title: At 35, there is still no end in sight for Dane Gagai
text:
He might be 35 and in his 16th year of NRL football, but Dane Gagai is not old.

Is he older than other players? Yes, definitely. Gagai has been around long enough that he's faced footballers involved in the Super League war.

He's the last Newcastle Knight to have played alongside Danny Buderus and when he moves to Brisbane next season he'll join Ben Hunt as the last Broncos to have played with Darren Lockyer.

Penrith legend Craig Gower, who made his first-grade debut 30 years ago, is another former teammate and Gagai is the only player in the entire league who has played in a preliminary final for the Knights courtesy of their run through the 2013 finals.

Dane Gagai is one of the NRL's longest-serving players. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Cody Hopwood, a teammate for Friday night's sudden-death semi-final against South Sydney, watched those games under a Knights blanket at his grandmother's house because he was just seven years old at the time.

Gagai is the fourth most-capped player in Knights history with 238 appearances and has already played the most first-grade games of any outside back in the history of the sport in Australia with 336 and counting.

But that doesn't mean he's old, not by a long shot, because in rugby league to be old is to be done and Gagai is far from done.

Dane Gagai will return to Brisbane next year after leaving almost 16 years ago. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

"If you call me old and I'm out on that field and I'm leaving you behind, whether it's fitness games, conditioning or in the weight room, you better back it up," Gagai said.

"I've signed another contract for next year and I don't plan on finishing up after that but whether that's the end or not, you only have a limited time in this game.

"I don't want to leave it and think, 'If only I'd put in a bit more here or there.'

"Like a lot of players say, you're a long time retired so you might as well enjoy it while you're here.

"It's that competitive side of me [that gets going] when people tell me I'm getting old. It gives me a point to prove."

Gagai has been proving that point for many years now as part of a long goodbye with no end in sight.

Dane Gagai has played some of his best football in recent years. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

It's a different world from the old days of "Origin Gagai", when he shrugged off indifferent club form to become a Queensland superhero.

For many years Gagai has worked hard to make the most of every moment and he still pushes himself to new limits at an age when other players are slowing down.

This year Gagai had the eighth-most tackle busts of any player in the league and was second only to Herbie Farnworth among centres.

He set a new career high for linebreaks in a season two years ago and recorded his career high for average metres per game the year before that.

Some of his best days have come when Newcastle have had little else to go on. Along with Jacob Saifiti, Gagai is one of just two players remaining at the club since its interminable one-win wooden spoon season in 2016.

Hard times like that have made him stronger.

Dane Gagai has given his all for the Knights, in good times and bad. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Case in point was last year, when the Knights again slumped to last amid a horror campaign beset by misery and blighted by attacking struggles.

On a team that couldn't attack to save itself, Gagai had the second-most tackle busts of any player in the league as he gave fine service for a hopeless cause right to the end.

This year, where the Knights have surged back into the finals despite another torrid injury toll, is both a reward and a vindication of his approach, a reminder that while winning is nice the fighting is the point.

Because of those injuries, a lot of Gagai's younger teammates have had to grow up quickly. Many of them will be making their finals debuts on Friday night and Gagai will offer advice if required, but to him most of them won't need it.

Crook elbows and big dreams propel unheralded Knights for finals Newcastle forward Francis Manuleleua might be less than two weeks off dislocating his right elbow but at the end of an interview he'll still shake your hand and shake it hard.

"I don't think I need to say much. I've been so impressed with how these young boys have stepped up," Gagai said.

"I'm sure the nerves are through the roof but nerves aren't always a bad thing. It's just about making sure you prepare well, that's what I'd say to the boys.

"Not only on the field but away from the field, be it sleep, diet, just doing everything you need to do to make sure, come Friday night, you have no doubt in your mind.

"You'll never be able to control nerves, they'll always be there. I still get them. Trust your ability, because these guys have shown what they're capable of and that doesn't change Friday night."

Sixteen years and 336 games is a long time to carry nerves around and they might be warranted this week given Gagai will be marking up on Latrell Mitchell, the apex predator of South Sydney's lethal left edge.

But Gagai learned how to turn those nerves into steel many years ago and he'll take a sense of certainty into his battle with Mitchell, where his physicality and decision-making will prove crucial to Newcastle's hopes of pulling off the upset.

"The nerves, for me, show that you care and you're worried about what could happen," Gagai said.

"But then you need to find out how to control what you can control. We know what Latrell is capable of, we know what Cody [Walker] is capable of, but I can't control what they do.

"I can only control what I do, how I go about things, what my actions are. That's one way to control those nerves, even if they'll always be there."

Dane Gagai still has plenty of mates at South Sydney. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

It'd be easy for Gagai to give into nostalgia this week of all weeks. He still has plenty of mates at South Sydney from his Rabbitoh days who he speaks with all the time. Gagai was shaking hands and slapping backs with a fair few of them at Jai Arrow's 100th NRL game last week.

He thinks Alex Johnston's record-breaking try this year was one of rugby league's best moments of the season and was proud to play a part in a few of them.

Gagai loves that he and his old teammates can fight like demons and have a laugh about it once the dust settles and the blood dries up, like he did after his memorable running battle with Cameron Munster in a match against the Storm earlier this year.

Perhaps he will swap jerseys with someone, as he has many times this year, building a collection he can one day see hanging on the walls and in which he can lose himself in memories.

But not yet. Gagai will not surrender himself to thinking of days past and the recollection of old friends and foes alike. There are still great things to come, he is sure of it.

Why Alex Johnston's record try was pure humanity After all the speculation, the fans stormed the field in the aftermath of Alex Johnston's record-breaking try and the result was an outpouring of emotion celebrating a once-in-a-lifetime achievement.

Gagai insists he has never given a single thought to retirement, or to how Friday could be his last game as a Knight, or to what awaits beyond his return to Brisbane, because to look back is to not be here and not being here is to be lost.

There is still plenty of fight in Gagai yet, especially if someone is going to call him old.

"It's that competitive side of me and I love that side, when people tell me something and I have a point to prove, not to anybody else, just to myself," Gagai said.

"Until I lose that passion, that motivation to compete and play our game, or if the body can't physically keep up, I'm not going to let anyone decide when I'm going to retire. That's my decision and my family's decision.

"I love playing rugby league, I love competing and I hate losing and I'm just glad I'm in this position where we can compete for a premiership."

title: Pocock slams multimillion-dollar report for Canberra precinct
text:
A new plan for the future of Canberra's Bruce precinct has been met with mixed reactions.

The suburb of Bruce is 15 minutes north of Canberra's CBD and home to North Canberra Hospital, the Australian Institute of Sport (AIS), the Canberra Stadium, and a Canberra Institute of Technology (CIT) campus, as well as medium-density dwellings.

But a 138-page Bruce Precinct Master Plan, written by consultants Hatch and Stantec and paid for by the federal government as part of a $10-million-dollar funding package, has been slammed as "a plan to make a plan".

"They don't provide a detailed business case or delivery plan. They don't resolve the Commonwealth-ACT government land issues. There's no costs. There's no implementation timetable," Independent ACT senator David Pocock said.

"I hope this isn't $10 million worth of work," he said.

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr said his government will prioritise health, education and transport in the precinct. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

But Senator Pocock's concerns over the plan's price tag were swiftly rebuffed by ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr.

"The $10 million extends beyond the master plan work," Mr Barr told 666 ABC Canberra.

" So let's put to bed this fallacy that's been running, kicked along by some in the political sphere. "

He said the report had cost about $4 million while $6 million had already been set aside for stadium upgrades.

"It's a complete replacement of the field-of-play lighting, an upgrade of public amenities at the venue, including the bathroom facilities, seating and lifts in the grandstands," Mr Barr said.

A perennial Canberra question

In March, Canberra Raiders coach Ricky Stuart unleashed his latest criticism of the state of his team's home venue, labelling it a "s***house stadium" after his Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs counterpart sliced his hand open.

The Raiders coach is among many Canberrans who have long asked: What's next for Bruce Stadium?

The ACT government had long ago quashed hopes for a new rectangular stadium to be built in the city, saying that the prospect of a new stadium in Civic had been "thoroughly explored".

ACT Chief Minister Andrew Barr says it's unlikely a decision will be made on a site for a new stadium until the end of this decade. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The Bruce Precinct Master Plan has offered two scenarios for a new stadium: building it in the same spot or putting it on the CIT campus.

The report does not suggest a preferred outcome.

And while some could see that as indecision, Mr Barr said it meant site options had now been drastically narrowed down to only two choices.

"The decision on this would be made towards the end of this decade and construction in the 2030s," he said.

The plan's first scenario imagines a new Canberra Stadium on the CIT site. (Supplied: Hatch and Stantec)

The plan's second scenario suggests a new Canberra Stadium could be constructed at the same spot. (Supplied: Hatch and Stantec)

Mr Barr said out of all the major infrastructure in the Bruce precinct, the stadium was not the highest priority.

"So, can I be crystal clear here about the hierarchy and what's most important?" Mr Barr asked.

"Health, education, housing, transport, and then we get to the sports facilities," he answered.

Under the master plan, the area surrounding the stadium would also be home to high-density housing, including towers up to 20 storeys tall.

Nearby Bruce village would feature housing ranging between six to 10 storeys in height.

The release of the master plan was timed with ACT Labor Senator Katy Gallagher and others speaking at the AIS about work getting underway, which the Commonwealth had already announced funding for more than two years ago.

$250 million had been earmarked for AIS accommodation, a sports dome and a new training centre.

title: Peter FitzSimons tells court Jones complainant was 'revolted' over claims
text:
Author and journalist Peter FitzSimons has begun to give evidence in Alan Jones's criminal trial, telling the court a young colleague of Mr Jones appeared "deeply upset" while detailing allegations of indecent assault.

Mr Jones has pleaded not guilty to 22 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching relating to six men, including a younger colleague, Complainant C, who has alleged the "powerful" broadcaster kissed and touched him multiple times.

The NSW Local Court trial on Thursday heard from Peter FitzSimons, a former Australian representative rugby union player-turned-journalist, who said he first met Mr Jones in 1982 when Mr Jones was coaching rugby.

He said he answered Mr Jones's call to join the Manly rugby league club and described the defendant as a "brilliant rugby league coach".

After writing two articles for the Sydney Morning Herald in 2017 about Mr Jones's "genius" in rugby coaching, Mr FitzSimons said he received a "very strong email from a young man".

It is not suggested that young man was Complainant C.

Alan Jones pictured outside court on Thursday morning. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

The journalist has been called to give evidence about a conversation he had with Complainant C in October 2019, a day after 2GB shock jock Ray Hadley informed him that a younger colleague wanted to speak about his experience with Mr Jones.

Mr FitzSimons said he spoke to Complainant C as arranged, and the man allegedly told him Mr Jones would "scrape or hold his penis" while in the car together, and kissed him in the lift to his Circular Quay apartment.

'He was revolted'

Mr FitzSimons said the complainant described Mr Jones as "the most important powerful person at 2GB" and was "drawn in" to Mr Jones's orbit.

"He couldn't quite believe that in the world that he was in … the number one person was noticing him," Mr FitzSimons said.

" He made clear … he was revolted by what had happened, but he was deeply upset at himself for not being stronger. "

He said Complainant C told him he did not say no to Mr Jones at the time, but did push his hand away.

The journalist told the court he immediately passed his notes from the phone call onto his colleague, investigative reporter Kate McClymont, because it appeared "extremely important".

"It was not a story I could possibly pursue on my own," he said.

Mr FitzSimons passed notes from a call with Complainant C onto his colleague. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Mr FitzSimons said four days after the phone conversation, Mr Hadley indicated Complainant C was "deeply upset", "panicking" and "spiralling", and he made it clear neither he nor Ms McClymont would pursue the story further at that time.

Defence argues alleged collusion

Under cross-examination, defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC questioned Mr FitzSimons about whether Mr Hadley "offered himself" as a source against Mr Jones as well as putting him in touch with Complainant C.

She put to him that Mr Hadley brought up the names of two other younger men in relation to Mr Jones, which Mr FitzSimons agreed with.

"[Ray Hadley] made allegations of sexual interaction with [one man] but I don't remember sexual allegations with [another man], but I remember his name coming up," he said.

The defence case is that Mr FitzSimons and Mr Hadley "colluded" by getting Complainant C to help "destroy" Mr Jones.

Ms Bashir put to Mr FitzSimons that he had a long standing and public dislike of Mr Jones.

She read back to the journalist some critical quotes from his stories about Mr Jones, including a quote that he was, "a tumour on the body politic of this city, state and country and the sooner he is excised the better".

"I am very proud of that quote," Mr FitzSimons replied.

Mr FitzSimons said it was "absolutely correct" that he "violently disagreed with Mr Jones" on many things, and he agreed he accused the broadcaster of "bullying", "lies" and "agendas".

Under cross examination, Mr FitzSimons said several times he did not understand the defence's question, sometimes speaking across Ms Bashir as she questioned him about an inconsistency between his evidence and his police statement.

"I am under oath confused," Mr FitzSimons appealed to Judge Glenn Walsh.

The trial continues.

title: Premier says Olympic rowing concerns 'last hurrah' of 'naysayers'
text:
Queensland's top political brass has flown to Rockhampton to again attempt to quash any concerns around the city's accommodation capacity to host an Olympic sporting event.

The central Queensland city was last year announced as the host for rowing and canoeing for the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games but it has been subject to debate since.

On Thursday morning, amid a gathering of rowing fraternity, tourism bodies, sporting groups and local politicians, Premier David Crisafulli stood on the bank of the Fitzroy River to double down on his commitment that the state government "was not for turning" on this.

"It's about a region who deserves a fair share," he said.

"In many ways, this fight symbolises that.

"Central Queenslanders are going to prove a whole heap of people from interstate and overseas wrong because it will be world-class and it will be generational and there will be legacy."

International rowing bodies have questioned the location's suitability for competition. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

International and national rowing bodies have raised concerns over the river's suitability, most recently at last week's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam.

Mr Crisafulli labelled critics "naysayers" and said concerns raised over the past 12 months, including over the natural river course, flooding, crocodiles, infrastructure and racing conditions, had already been "debunked easily".

"Every so-called impediment that's been put up has been dismissed," he said.

"This is the last hurrah of people trying to find ways to discredit something that makes a hell of a lot of sense.

" We're not for turning on this. "

When questioned whether Rockhampton's selection was part of a strategy to shore up electorates in the region, the premier pointed to the many regions set to host events, including sailing in Townsville in the Whitsundays, equestrian in Toowoomba, football in Cairns, and archery in Maryborough.

The venue still needs approval from World Rowing. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

Accommodation concerns

This week, media outlets also reported on further concerns around a lack of accommodation in the city, citing complaints Rowing Queensland had received from parents struggling to find accommodation ahead of next weekend's Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta.

The region's peak tourism body, Capricorn Enterprise, has flagged in recent years the need for an extra 1,200 short-term accommodation rooms by 2032, for current and future demand, not including Olympic tourism requirements.

"We have lost short-term accommodation rooms to long-term rentals because of the housing shortage, [but] that's now starting to be relieved a bit because houses are coming out of the ground pretty quickly" the body's chief executive, Mary Carroll, said.

"We just don't have enough rooms. I'm desperate for more accommodation rooms in the next six years."

Tony Williams has thanked the state government for its support of Olympic rowing in the city. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie argued the Olympic event would drive investment in the accommodation sector, with planning work also underway for a 1,200-bed athlete's village.

Highlighting a shed at the rowing course, built after the Canadian Olympic team trained on the Fitzroy River ahead of the 2000 Sydney Olympics, he said the legacy would be long-lasting in terms of accommodation and housing.

"The campaign that's being run at the moment — that there's not enough accommodation — that same campaign was run months ago in Brisbane, that's why we're unlocking land," Mr Bleijie said.

Both men pointed to the city hosting Beef Australia every three years, which brought 125,000 extra people to the city.

Simon Irwin says the region is capable of hosting large-scale events. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

Beef Australia chief executive Simon Irwin said 35,000 people went through turnstiles of the event's first day.

"We do that in an environment where we have filled every possible piece of accommodation in central Queensland, almost down to Gladstone nowadays," Mr Irwin said.

He said he had been in contact with the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA) explaining the way the organisation handled the influx.

"The idea that we need to be able to place 25,000 people here is not new," he said.

"It happens on the first Monday in May every three years and we're more than happy to share that information and show that it can be done."

In previous years, the event has relied on residents renting out their homes for accommodation, temporary campsites near the event and even charter flights for day visits from other regional cities.

David Crisafulli says all technical assessments of the river are heading in the right direction. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

The venue still needs approval from the sport's governing body, World Rowing.

Mr Crisafulli reiterated his confidence in the river's suitability.

"The technical assessments are all heading in the right direction and that's repeatedly what we're being told," he said.

He also confirmed the results from the assessment would be made publicly available.

President of Rockhampton Fitzroy Rowing Club Sarah Black says the Olympics will bring great benefits to local rowers. (ABC Capricornia: Jacob Gamble)

title: Melbourne's NFL game is a battle of opposing jet lag strategies
text:
Two enormously well-resourced teams; two diametrically opposed strategies for managing one of the world's most arduous sporting road trips.

On Friday, the Los Angeles Rams will 'host' the San Francisco 49ers in the first NFL regular-season match played in Australia, at the local time of 10:35am in Melbourne.

That is 5:35pm on Thursday in Los Angeles, roughly equivalent to when a prime-time NFL fixture would kick off on the west coast of America.

Everything you need to know about NFL Melbourne The San Francisco 49ers are taking on the Los Angeles Rams at the MCG, the first NFL regular-season game to be held in Australia. Here's everything you need to know.

To prepare, the 49ers flew in a week earlier and have embarked on a series of PR appearances across the city — lauding local baristas and watching Geelong defeat Carlton in an AFL final — while the Rams arrived this morning, just 24 hours before the historic clash.

The Rams' strategy is not without precedent; last year they flew to London on the day of their game against the Jaguars and came away with a 35-7 win, returning home without needing to stay in a hotel.

The Los Angeles side will be hoping for a repeat of that result, only this time they will contend with a 16-hour flight and 17-hour time difference, and cannot avoid an overnight stay.

Both teams have opted to return as soon as possible after the game, as they prepare for week two fixtures back in the United States.

Only one strategy can prevail, with the NFL an invested onlooker.

NFL chief medical Officer Allen Sills is in Melbourne for the Rams and 49ers clash. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Maximilian Haupt)

Allen Sills, the NFL's chief medical officer, confirmed that both teams had engaged sleep experts to strategise on their approach, albeit with different outcomes.

"We don't have a league mandate [on what teams should do]," Dr Sills said.

"Frankly, it often has to do with how successful the team is. If the team did it one way and won, they'll tend to do that the next time they do it."

While the NFL is keeping a close eye on injury rates, Dr Sills said the league did not have enough data to prefer one strategy.

"We've tried to share data, but the problem is, we've had such a small number of injuries relative to the number of games that we have played [internationally], that we can't say, coming in this day versus that day is clearly different for injury.

"They're two very different approaches this year, so we're all interested in [the outcome]."

49ers using ‘gradual adjustment’ strategy

With two sets of experts advising the teams, the obvious question is: how did they come up with such different strategies?

"Each has a rationale, and either strategy is valid," said David Cunnington, an Australian-based sleep physician with over 20 years' experience in clinical practice.

The 49ers chose to acclimatise to Melbourne's time zone. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

As Dr Cunnington explained, teams can optimise performance in two ways: by syncing players' body clocks to their destination, or "keeping their body clocks in sync with their home time zone and just ducking out and playing the game in a different time zone, and then ducking back to their time zone".

The former strategy — favoured by the 49ers — requires time, a luxury most 'ordinary' travellers do not have.

"It's really going to be dependent on whether you have a spare week to acclimatise," Dr Cunnington said.

He has a 'rough and ready' rule for how many time zones you can adjust to per 24 hours.

If you are travelling west (going 'forward' in time) — such as from Los Angeles to Melbourne — you can theoretically adjust by two time zones per day.

So if Melbourne is seven time zones west of Los Angeles, you would need at least four days of adjustment time (the 49ers have allowed five).

Loading Instagram content

When choosing this strategy, Dr Cunnington advised having daily goals to incrementally adjust to the new time zone. For example, you might bring your bed and wake times forward by two hours per day.

Key to this working is adjusting your light exposure. As Dr Cunnington explained, you want to avoid exposure to light when it is your 'rest' or 'bed' time, and introduce artificial light when it is time to get up.

This is a strategy Dr Sills confirmed the NFL teams had employed.

"Our teams have engaged sleep experts to craft an individualised plan for the players starting from two weeks leading up to the game for how they should alter their sleep and light exposure," he said.

As examples, athletes may use devices like sleep masks or noise-cancelling headphones to minimise sensory input when they need to wind down or sleep, and blue light glasses to introduce light when they should be waking up.

Rams' strategy may have edge, says sleep expert

In the case of two major NFL franchises, both teams are working with significant budgets — including private jets — that allow them to control as many travel variables as possible.

Head coach Sean McVay and the LA Rams have left it as late as they could before arriving in Melbourne for their clash with the 49ers. (Getty Images: LA Times/Ronaldo Bolaños)

In the Rams' case, they have announced that players will be travelling on 'lie-flat' beds for their last-minute trip to Melbourne, alleviating one of travel's most burdensome problems: sleeping on a plane.

"People will definitely sleep better lying flat than propped upright," Dr Cunnington said, adding that this was mostly habitual.

However, it is not a foolproof strategy.

"Sleep loss is one of the challenges or cons of the Rams' strategy," he said.

"If you happen not to sleep well on the flight, you can't make that up if you're just flying in and out.

"Whereas for the 49ers, if they don't sleep well, they've got a week to acclimatise, have some naps, and make up that sleep."

Nonetheless, when pressed, Dr Cunnington said he would choose the Rams' strategy over the 49ers.

He justified this by saying it worked for the team previously, and they do not have to 're-adjust' to Los Angeles time once they return.

In addition, with the Melbourne game being played at 10:35am, they have the advantage of it being in a familiar local time slot.

"The 49ers are adjusting to Melbourne time, but when they're [back home] they wouldn't play 10am games. All their games are in the afternoon or evenings, so by acclimatising to Melbourne time, they're actually playing at a different time to what their body clocks are used to."

NFL monitoring injury risk associated with travel

Whatever the outcome, the NFL has invested significant resources into ensuring its players make it through the game unscathed.

They have employed 30 medical staff for game day, including 12 from The Alfred Hospital, to be on stand-by.

This is in part to appease the teams who make the long trek in the aim of sending the franchise international, with head of NFL International Gerrit Meier telling Reuters the players need to return "healthy" for the code to consider returning to Australia.

Dr Cunnington said there was some merit to the fear of player injury after a long-haul flight, and associated jet lag.

"There is an increased risk [of injury], but not directly," he said.

"It's not as if jet lag causes injury, but I like to think of it as a predisposition to clumsiness. Just not being quite as coordinated, and then via that mechanism, having a risk of injury."

Some — like 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan — have expressed cynicism about international travel, previously saying the San Franciscan team was "fired up" about having two international fixtures in one year.

"I think our coaches very much like routine and crave consistency of things, and international travel is always a variance," Dr Ellis said.

"What I would tell you is that we've seen players really enjoy the experience when they come over, and see the passion and energy of the fans and the enthusiasm of the countries we've been in.

"The league is always evaluating each venue, and there's so much that goes into that. Health and safety is an important part of that … we always look at injuries associated with international games, and that's an ongoing effort."

title: Have you made one of these six travel mistakes?
text:
There's nothing quite like a well-earned break.

But whether you are driving to your nearest beach town or embarking on an adventure via a long-haul flight, simple mistakes can make a holiday memorable for all the wrong reasons.

Here are some common errors and how you can avoid them.

An overloaded and inflexible itinerary

When travelling, people often rush around, seeing as much as possible, says Michael Turtle, a travel writer and blogger who lives on Gadigal land in Sydney.

"[But] you're just so exhausted by the end of the day that you just don't enjoy it."

And you also risk becoming run-down, he says.

"The best way to approach holidays — especially one that involves a bit of sightseeing — is to basically have one or two main tentpole activities for the day," Mr Turtle suggests.

This could be as simple as planning a morning and an afternoon activity and letting "those serendipitous moments" fall into place around them, he says.

Lauren McRae, a travel agent who lives in the NSW border town of Albury, on the traditional lands of the Wiradjuri people, also recommends building in flexibility and breathing space in your schedule.

For example, she says the weather in Bali might mean you wait until the day before to book an activity, like an ATV (all-terrain vehicle) tour.

However, Ms McRae says to pre-book anything you would be heartbroken to miss.

Booking unsuitable accommodation

Lucas Brancatisano says he's made the mistake of booking "rubbish" accommodation to save money.

Mr Brancatisano makes social media content about his travels and lives in the Gold Coast/Yugambeh language region.

Sometimes the accommodation is cheaper because the area is further away from the things you want to see and do, but you end up spending more on transport, he says.

Often, the budget price reflects the quality and "you really quickly realise why it's so cheap".

Spending an extra 10 or 15 dollars a night in some places can result in an "infinitely better experience", Mr Brancatisano says.

Ms McRae says bed configurations and capacity in hotels and resorts can cause unexpected problems, particularly for families.

You might assume you can ask for a roll-away bed on arrival, but hotel policies and even legal requirements mean it's better to check in advance, she says.

"A lot of places in Fiji and even Bali will allow two children under 12 to stay in the room for free. However, it's based on existing bedding."

Michael Turtle says the best accommodation to book can depend on your mode of transport and how accessible a destination is. (Supplied: Michael Turtle)

Packing too much

"I'm a chronic over-packer myself," Mr Brancatisano admits.

But he's learnt that unless you're going somewhere very remote, you can usually buy something you need.

"Go in with a lighter bag. If you can do just carry-on, honestly that's the way to go," he says.

Jetstar to charge new fees for overhead baggage Jetstar has announced it will charge passengers to stow carry-on luggage in overhead lockers from next year, allowing only a small under-seat bag at no extra cost.

Bringing along too many shoes is an easy blunder that adds weight and bulk to your luggage. He recommends taking no more than three pairs.

Ms McRae says "overpacking is a big mistake" as it wastes time and precious space.

If you're flying with checked luggage, Ms McRae and Mr Turtle suggest packing everything you would need for a day or so in your carry-on in case your checked luggage is delayed or lost.

This is particularly important if you take medication, they say.

When he was a less-experienced traveller, Lucas Brancatisano (right) says he would worry, "What if I need this?" (Supplied: Lucas Brancatisano )

Failing to notify your bank or compare exchange rates and fees

Forgetting to let your bank know you're heading overseas can disrupt your trip, Ms McRae says.

What are your options when taking money overseas? When it comes to planning an overseas trip, deciding how you're going to access your money can seem overwhelming. Experts outline your options.

"They might flag that as a suspicious transaction and freeze your card, leaving you with no access to money until you call them and try and get it reactivated, which can take time," she says.

Ms McRae says your ordinary card could also come with high international transaction and ATM fees.

She uses a travel card instead.

Mr Brancatisano also prefers a travel card and suggests doing a little research beforehand to compare options, including their exchange rates and ATM fees.

Not checking your passport details

If you're heading overseas, Ms McRae urges you to check your passport's expiration date.

"For most destinations when you're leaving Australia, you need to have at least six months' validity on your passport — especially for Bali."

Another mistake Ms McRae hears about often is when the name on someone's passport doesn't match their flight booking.

"When you're booking flights, you need to have your name as per passport on the ticket."

Late visa applications

Mr Turtle once applied for an ESTA (electronic system for travel authorisation) just within the recommended 72-hour window before travelling into the United States, but it didn't come through in time, and he missed his flight.

Lauren McRae says she recently helped someone who thought they could get a visa into Vietnam on arrival, which used to be the case. (Supplied: Lauren McRae)

Ms McRae recommends checking entry requirements before you book as they may have changed since you last travelled.

For example, the United Kingdom introduced an electronic travel authorisation (ETA) for Australian travellers last January, while Australian travellers to Bali need a health declaration (the All Indonesia Declaration Form), a visa and a tourist levy to enter.

Forgetting about insurance

"Always have travel insurance, regardless of where you're going," Mr Turtle says.

Ms McRae suggests taking out a travel insurance policy as soon as you pay for any expenses.

Lucas Brancatisano says sorting out travel insurance is a must. (Supplied: Lucas Brancatisano)

"You could come down with an illness, break your leg or something unforeseen might happen and … if you don't have travel insurance, then all those restrictive terms and conditions come into play, and you could lose thousands of dollars," she says.

Ms McRae recommends checking the amount of cover, that any pre-existing health conditions are not exempt and that all destinations and activities are covered.

She adds that there can be an extra premium for skiing or going on a cruise.

Mr Brancatisano says travel insurance is an essential.

"You can get through unscathed, but you don't want to be caught out if you don't have it."

title: Australia's most expensive homes decline in value
text:
Australia's most expensive homes are declining in value, with high-end houses in Sydney and Melbourne down more than 10 per cent from peak levels.

Homes valued in the top 25 per cent have dropped 10.7 per cent below peak levels in Sydney and 10.5 per cent in Melbourne, according to property data.

Cotality's September housing charts, which track housing value movement, reported that the median value of these expensive homes is $2.1 million in Sydney and $1.2 million in Melbourne.

However, lower-priced homes and units have continued to show greater resilience, it found.

Home values decline in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth

Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said the decline had spread beyond Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra, which were the first cities to turn and continued to record the largest cumulative falls.

"More recently, however, home values have also started declining across Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth, demonstrating that the downturn is now affecting a broader range of markets," he said.

Homes valued in the top 25 per cent have dropped 10.7 per cent below peak levels in Sydney. (ABC News: Jak Rowland)

In contrast, price declines across Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth have been more evenly distributed across all price points, reflecting their later entry into the downturn, he said.

Herron Todd White group CEO Peter Maloney said buyers at the top end of the market generally had greater capacity to delay a purchase, while sellers could take longer to adjust their expectations.

"But it's important not to treat prestige property as one national market," he said.

Peter Maloney says the downturn in property prices is due to a multitude of reasons. (Supplied)

National annual sales fall

Australian Centre for Housing Research director Emma Baker said the correction in the market had mostly affected investors.

"Some of it, I suspect, is investors stepping back and waiting to see what happens," she said.

The professor said home buyers were in the market for a different reason and that they were less concerned with financial strategy and waiting to see how the federal governments tax changes play out.

"Especially at the lower end of the market … a household looking for a relatively affordable home often still needs somewhere to live and has a fairly narrow part of the market it can realistically buy into," she said.

"At the higher end, buyers are more able to delay, compromise or simply decide that a property is not worth the asking price."

Here's how the budget's tax changes will affect you Answers to all your questions about the federal budget's changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax.

National annual sales fell by 2.7 per cent over the year to August, with capital cities down 5.2 per cent, the Cotality data shows.

Meanwhile, regional sales rose 1.8 per cent, but Professor Baker said localities classed as regional varied widely, and included areas close to major cities and large regional cities.

Open home attendance rates, however, suggest the premium end is beginning to turn.

Ray White Group chief economist Nerida Conisbee said the number of people attending open homes halved between January and July this year.

"Since then, the decline has stopped and attendance has edged back up," she said.

Attendance is still weaker than earlier in the year, but buyer demand is no longer deteriorating at the same pace, the economist said.

Housing downturn linked to many factors

Low-priced houses and units continue to show resilience. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Mr Maloney said affordability was stretched, borrowing costs remained elevated and, in several markets, buyers then had more stock to choose from.

"When buyers become more cautious and have more choice, they are less willing to chase a vendor's price," he said.

"That shifts negotiating power towards the buyer and can put downward pressure on values."

Unit market value also downtrending

Mr Burg said a similar trend was evident across the unit market.

"[But] units have generally proven more resilient throughout the downturn, supported by their relative affordability and lower entry price points," he said.

"While higher value units have generally recorded larger declines than lower value stock, the gap is smaller than what we are seeing across detached housing."

Housing affordability at all-time low Housing affordability has fallen to the lowest rate on record, with households earning a typical income only able to afford around one in every 10 properties sold last financial year.

According to Mr Burg, Canberra's unit market had "bucked the pattern", with lower-value units recording larger declines than higher-value ones.

Units valued in the lowest 25 per cent in Canberra are down 2.9 per cent from peak levels, compared with a 1.6 per cent decline across higher-value units.

The data showed the difference between unit value decline in the highest and lowest 25 per cent was widest in Melbourne and Sydney, at 4.9 and 4.5 per cent.

But Perth's unit market recorded larger declines than houses across every price point, while Adelaide's most expensive units fell further than its highest-value houses, Mr Burg said.

"Despite these exceptions, affordability has generally helped support demand for units and cushion value declines relative to detached housing," he said.

title: F1 debuts a new track with a corner so grand it is called Monumental
text:
Formula 1 debuts a new circuit to its calendar, and despite no grand prix raced yet, the Madring already boasts a corner that is poised to become an iconic scene in motorsport.

The Spanish Grand Prix has moved from Barcelona to the nation's capital, Madrid, with the brand-new Madring contracted to host the event until 2035.

Schumacher comparisons made as Antonelli continues historic F1 season Kimi Antonelli's win from 19th on the grid in Monza was epic, and the way his rivals raced with him has drawn comparisons with Ferrari legend Michael Schumacher.

The track uses a combination of public roads and private land and will at times reflect a street circuit, and other times a permanent race track.

But the defining feature of this 22-corner circuit is turn 12: La Monumental.

Turn 12 is a long, banked hairpin that promises to be unlike anything in F1 currently.

The 270-degree curve will have banking up to 13.5 degrees, not as dramatic as the 18-degrees of banking at Zandvoort, but this corner will be taken at much higher speed.

Williams driver Carlos Sainz drove around the circuit earlier this year in a Ford Mustang GT, and said he expects F1 cars to be flying around La Monumental.

"My feeling is the corner is going to be flat out the whole way, and it's going to create an overtaking opportunity into the next tight left," he said.

"The banking will allow you to maybe position the car higher up or lower down if you want to get clean air to follow.

"But if it's easy flat, then it will also be a corner where if you stay tight, you will produce quite a bit of slipstream, like you see in Zandvoort."

Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli enters this weekend with a 66-point lead in the drivers' championship over teammate George Russell, after a stunning win in Italy last Sunday despite starting 19th on the grid.

Australian Oscar Piastri is seventh in the drivers' championship, 151 points behind Antonelli, and placed fifth last Sunday at the Italian Grand Prix.

title: At least five dead, 87 missing as Philippine ferry catches fire
text:
At least five people are dead and 87 remain unaccounted-for after a fire erupted aboard a ferry near a tourist hotspot in the Philippines province of Palawan, officials say.

The fire aboard the MV June Aster broke out on Wednesday evening, local time, 2.2 kilometres offshore, the coastguard said, adding that five casualties had been brought ashore.

Video shared by the Philippine Coast Guard on social media showed the ferry completely engulfed by flames.

Video showed the ferry ablaze off the coast of Palawan. (Philippine Coast Guard (PCG)/AFP)

Coast guard personnel tossed life jackets to survivors as the ferry burnt.

Images shared by the coastguard showed passengers helped into smaller boats and taken to shallow water, and body bags were laid out at what looked like a port.

"Based on the data we have right now on rescued and the casualties, we still have 87 people who are unaccounted-for," Philippine Coast Guard Captain Noemi Cayabyab told a local radio station on Thursday.

She said 42 people had been rescued and that the ship's manifest listed 117 passengers and 17 crew.

A survivor is helped off a small boat after being rescued from a burning ferry off Palawan province, Philippines. (AP: Philippine Coast Guard)

"Just to make it clear, this is live data and may change as our search and rescue operations are ongoing," Captain Cayabyab said.

Of those rescued, 38 were passengers and four were crew, she said.

Bad weather and big waves were challenging rescuers, and sea currents had dragged the ferry several nautical miles from its initial location, she said.

Captain Cayabyab said it was still unclear what caused the fire and the coast guard is coordinating with the shipping company and maritime authorities to get more details.

title: Dementia prevention too heavily focused on personal choices, study finds
text:
Personal preventative measures alone will not decrease the risk of dementia, researchers have found.

Until now there has been a focus on personal choices such as eating, exercise, social activity and mental health to prevent Australia's leading cause of death.

But a Dementia Australia-funded research paper from Curtin University has found that such efforts may have led to the social, environmental and policy influences that shape brain health being overlooked.

In 2024, a landmark study identified 14 potentially modifiable risk factors for dementia, including high blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol, physical inactivity, smoking and hearing loss.

It found many must be tackled in midlife and could potentially prevent 45 per cent of dementia cases.

In the new paper published in the peer-reviewed medical journal The Lancet, researchers mapped 61 risk factors ranging from lifestyle to socio-economic status.

Of those, 49 (80 per cent) were at the individual level. Far fewer related to the interpersonal or societal levels.

The researchers found far less attention was paid to education, housing, neighbourhood safety, healthcare access, clean air and social connections, "despite growing evidence these factors affect people’s ability to protect their brain health".

"For example, we tell people they need to be physically active, but being physically active can depend on having a safe environment and access to places that are safe to exercise in and affordable," study author Jennifer Dunne said.

“[The 14 factors] are obviously important for a range of reasons, but our study shows that many of the factors that shape dementia risk do not sit solely within an individual’s control."

14 ways to cut dementia risk Many of the risk factors for dementia – being female, growing older and the genetic lottery — cannot be avoided. But research is uncovering a growing list of ways to cut your risk.

University of NSW cognitive disorder researcher Simone Reppermund, who was not involved in the study, said the paper highlighted the need for greater understanding of the role sociological, economic and environmental factors played in dementia prevention.

"Often the message goes out that it is actually on the individual to change something, but many important factors that actually are very much interlinked and interconnected with these individual behaviours are neglected or not even looked at in research, and especially in policy," she said.

"This is harder to do because it changes from society to society, and then you have high-income and low-income countries, but it is definitely an important way to go forward."

The dementia risk factors all Australians should know Too many Australians still see dementia as an inevitability, according to new data, but there is a list of steps you can take to reduce the risks.

About 446,500 people are living with dementia in Australia and that figure is projected to exceed one million by 2065, according to Dementia Australia.

Dementia is the decline in the ability to think, remember and reason to the extent that it interferes with a person's daily life and activities, the National Ageing Research Institute said.

"There is a lot more focus now on dementia and how to prevent it, because dementia is a huge economic burden, a huge health burden, and it affects not only the individual but the whole family and the whole society," Dr Reppermund said.

Dr Dunne said it hoped the latest research findings would inform prevention policy.

"The research has been very valuable to get us to this point," she said.

"What we're now saying is that it does need to go further, and that if we really want to be talking about preventing dementia and improving brain health at a population level, we need ot look at the whole population and how the individual lives within that."

title: Gold boom leaves little room for tourists in outback mining city
text:
The ongoing gold boom is starting to prove a headache for tourism in one of Australia's landmark mining cities.

With more than half a million passengers over the past 12 months, Kalgoorlie-Boulder Airport is one of the busiest in Western Australia outside of Perth.

But tour operators in the city, 600 kilometres east of Perth, say the mine workers accounting for the bulk of the passenger traffic are competing with other visitors for available accommodation.

With rents at historic highs and almost no vacancies, finding a place to stay is proving a challenge.

Tourism WA statistics show the region has had some of the highest hotel occupancy rates in the state during the 2025/2026 financial year.

The region's occupancy peaked in October 2025 with about 90 per cent of hotel rooms surveyed occupied.

One of Australia's largest open-cut mines, the Super Pit is a major draw for tourists. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Leanne Kamp has been running gold prospecting tours through the Goldfields for two decades.

While a jump in interest from would-be gold hunters has been good for business, she said it has never been tougher for travellers to find a room.

Leanne Kamp has been running tours in the Eastern Goldfields for two decades. (Supplied: Leanne Kamp)

"With the mining boom and all the fly-in, fly-out miners, it does really crunch into the available accommodation," she said.

"We always cross our fingers because the accommodation is quite difficult to find, and we find that we are booking about 12 months in advance."

Kalgoorlie's tourism numbers have been climbing in recent years. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Winter and spring are generally considered peak tourism season, with the Diggers and Dealers Mining Conference and Kalgoorlie-Boulder Race Round bringing thousands of visitors to the city.

Identified by Kalgoorlie-Boulder's Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KBCCI) as far back as 2022, the growing number of workers occupying previously short-stay accommodation has forced tourism operators to adopt creative solutions.

"Businesses and workers are increasingly relying on short-term accommodation, with examples of many short-stay establishments largely servicing workers," the KBCCI report stated.

Tourists and workers share space in the outback city of Kalgoorlie-Boulder. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Ms Kamp had to think quickly when accommodation arranged for a tour last year fell through.

"We brought tents over … we set up camp on one of our leases," she said.

Catching gold fever

There were about 120,000 domestic tourist trips to Kalgoorlie-Boulder and the surrounding region in 2025, according to Tourism WA figures.

The world's ongoing fascination with gold keeps businesses across the region regularly booked. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

In addition to the gold and mining, the city's rich history is a big attraction for visitors.

Sharon Ingham-Sellin is visiting Kalgoorlie from Mandurah with the Red Hat Society, a social club for women over 50.

Libby Clarke and Sharon Ingham-Sellin visited Kalgoorlie with the Red Hat Ladies from Mandurah. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

She managed to find accommodation, but only by booking several months in advance.

"It's an iconic town of WA and probably the whole country," Ms Sellen said.

" I'm really loving the historic buildings, food's been amazing, your pubs are amazing. "

Potential visitors lost

The shortage of rooms is taking a significant toll on mining engineer-turned-tour operator Allison Golsby.

"We are having people try to ring us and say 'How can we make this work?' particularly less than six weeks ahead and they're unable to get accommodation," she said.

Gold is a big drawcard for miners and tourists. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

"So that's really hard for our region and it's taking away some of the opportunities."

Ms Golsby said her tours were booked out months in advance, and believed the region was missing out on potential visitors.

Allison Golsby became a tour operator to show off the rugged beauty of the Eastern Goldfields. (Supplied: Allison Golsby)

"Think of those jobs, think of the prosperity," she said.

"Think of the things that we could do in our town with that type of thing coming through."

Could historic hotels help?

Despite the high demand and challenges, Kalgoorlie-Boulder's Visitor Centre is still encouraging people to come to town.

Centre manager Donna Malec agreed the accommodation crunch was holding the city's potential back.

She said she encouraged would-be visitors to be flexible with their dates, and the centre was always happy to help.

An aerial view of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine. (ABC Goldfields: Ivo Da Silva)

"We're trying our best to let people know, 'No, no, you can still come, it just might not be on the day that you want,'" she said.

"But if you're quite flexible with your time, we can always make something work for you."

Claire Smart manages daily bus tours to one of the largest open-cut gold mines in the world: Kalgoorlie's Super Pit.

Claire Smart runs tours into the Super Pit. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

She said historic hotels in Kalgoorlie-Boulder, now empty, could provide part of the answer.

"Old hotels would be a good one because there's a lot of history involved in that," Ms Smart said.

"And that's what a lot of the tourists come for; the history and just to see what's out there for Kalgoorlie-Boulder."

title: Audit finds Inpex has taken 'significant steps' to rectify emissions errors
text:
An independent audit has found Inpex is on track to fix major errors in reporting toxic emissions from its Ichthys LNG facility in Darwin, as the company faces prosecution and calls for better regulation.

Inpex emissions 'systematically underestimated' since 2018, report finds An independent review into oil and gas company Inpex has found widespread errors in emissions reporting.

The audit by consulting firm AECOM, ordered by the Northern Territory Environment Protection Authority (NT EPA) earlier in the year, found no evidence Inpex deliberately falsified emissions data and concluded the company had implemented "appropriate improvement actions" to better the accuracy of its reporting.

However, auditor Todd Mitchell noted that no independent site inspection was undertaken, and that his findings relied on publicly available documents and information provided by Inpex.

He also confirmed the company had not yet corrected all historical emissions errors and, despite making improvements, still does not directly measure all emission sources.

The audit found Inpex had not yet corrected all historical emissions errors. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Inpex is currently facing prosecution by the NT environmental regulator over its under-reporting of emissions, including benzene — a chemical classified by the World Health Organisation as a class 1 carcinogen.

The Japanese gas giant was due to make its first court appearance on Wednesday, but the matter was vacated until November.

Audit part of environmental crack down

In July, the NT EPA recommended changes — including pollution limits — to Inpex's licence, as the regulator attempted to crack down on the company.

As part of the NT EPA's multi-pronged approach, an environmental auditor was ordered to evaluate Inpex's ability to control pollution, examine whether it had taken actions to rectify potential harm from pollution, and whether the company was accurately reporting emissions to the National Pollutant Inventory.

"The auditor concludes that Inpex has taken significant steps to rectify its emissions under-reporting," the report states, but added "there is additional work to complete".

The report said Inpex is now counting emissions from gas ships while they are moored at the facility, but noted the company is using industry averages from the Emission Estimation Technique Manual for Maritime Operations instead of direct, on-the-ground measurements.

Emissions from gas ships moored at the Inpex facility are calculated using industry averages rather than on-the-ground measurements. (Supplied: Inpex Australia)

The auditor said he considered this an "appropriate methodology" in the absence of direct sampled ship emissions "noting ship emissions would vary between vessels".

Ammonia emissions, as well as fuel and condensate emissions, were also being counted.

The report said Inpex is transitioning from its in-house spreadsheet reporting tool to an "advanced" environmental data management system, which the auditor found would significantly reduce the risk of future reporting errors if implemented properly.

Some pollutants not being reported

The auditor also questioned whether Inpex was reporting all required pollutants and emissions.

He found that while Inpex was reporting emissions on the government's list of 93 pollutants which potentially pose a risk to humans or the environment, the auditor said it was "unclear whether a full review has been done".

He highlighted mercury — a toxic chemical — as an example of a pollutant that was not being reported across all sources at the facility.

The auditor questioned whether the gas giant's Darwin facility was reporting all required pollutants. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The audit identified multiple sources of "uncertainty" in the way emissions are reported, including the company's use of annual measurements which "may not fully capture variability".

Leaks and other fugitive emissions were recognised "as a key source of uncertainty", and the auditor pointed out that some emissions were still estimated using government averages rather than measured directly at the source.

However, he ultimately found the uncertainties "acceptable".

In a statement on Wednesday afternoon, the NT EPA confirmed Inpex had committed to implementing the auditor's recommendations, including undertaking an annual assurance assessment and updating all emission calculations.

NT Environment Centre climate campaigner Dan Broun said the audit makes it clear that Inpex's emissions were "yet to be rectified".

Environment groups say they are concerned about the potential impact of emissions on residents and the environment. (Flickr: Geoff Whalan)

"The fact that ongoing audits are required show that Inpex hasn't got a handle on the situation at Ichthys and must not be trusted when it comes to Darwin's air quality," he said.

" Inpex has an enormous amount of work to do to bring down its emissions, monitor them correctly, and report them accurately. "

Inpex senior vice president Bill Townsend said the audit highlights the actions the company took to address the unintended errors in the way some emissions were calculated and reported.

He said the safety and wellbeing of people, and the protection of the environment and community through safe operations, remain the highest priority.

"Importantly, ongoing air quality monitoring in the Darwin region has consistently shown emissions levels are well within government guidelines, meaning no increased health risk to the community, our local workforce or the environment from the Ichthys LNG facility," he said.

Western Australia’s peak mining and energy body remains firm that the state should remain separate from a national gas reservation scheme after the federal government released the proposed legislation for consultation. The Domestic Gas Reservation Bill 2026 aims to establish Australia’s first national gas reservation policy to secure local supply for Australians and put downward pressure on domestic prices. Chamber of Minerals and Energy Western Australia chief executive Aaron Morey. Trevor Collens The scheme requires exporters to supply a portion of the gas they produce to the domestic market, with the initial proposal looking to reserve up to 20 per cent of gas exports. However, Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive Aaron Morey believes the current state government policy remains the best option for West Australians.

Advertisement

Under legislation set out by the state government two decades ago, WA gas exporters are currently required to provide a 15 per cent proportion of their exports to the domestic market – although that figure is set over the life of a project, not an annual designation, which remains a point of contention. Morey said WA had the balance right in its domestic scheme. “We remain absolutely certain that the best thing for Western Australia is for it not to be included in this scheme,” he said. “[The WA policy] is a scheme that has flexibility at its heart, and that has resulted in a set of outcomes that has worked for everyone.” Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King said under the proposed scheme, domestic supply obligations must be met in the same market as the export facility.

Advertisement

“An eastern exporter cannot meet their obligations by selling gas into the western market,” she said. “In a market that is well supplied, the domestic supply obligation can be reduced. For example, if the western market were found to be well supplied, it would be possible for discretion to be applied to reduce that obligation to zero.” King said WA’s scheme was about ensuring the state was well provided for in terms of gas for households, but also manufacturing and refining. “Different providers there provide different amounts of gas and that’s all agreed with the state government,” she said. “If the state government is satisfied with that because it’s their obligation, they’ve taken that obligation earlier than anyone else to make sure that their citizens and their industry is supplied with gas.”

Advertisement

However, Greenpeace Australia Pacific WA campaigns lead Geoff Bice said the gas industry had been getting away with “daylight robbery” in WA for years. Related Article Gas Labor wants its 20 per cent gas reservation scheme to apply nationally. What does that mean for WA? “If the federal domestic reservation requirements are not made to apply here it is a major missed opportunity to rein them in,” he said. “If the federal government is not going to keep Woodside and the WA gas industry accountable, it is incumbent on the WA government to tighten its rules. “The WA government needs to get a fair deal for West Australians and rule out risking pristine environments like Scott Reef and the Kimberley for unnecessary gas expansion.”

Advertisement

A state government spokesperson said WA’s approach to domestic gas has worked for years to secure 20 per cent of export volumes for WA households and businesses. “We have consistently said to the federal government that they should carve our successful policy out of their scheme and not do anything that undermines investor confidence in the new projects that will meet our future domestic gas needs,” the spokesperson said. “We don’t want a policy designed to solve a problem on the east coast unintentionally costing jobs in WA. “We are carefully examining the exposure draft released today and consulting with industry. “We will respond in a considered way, and we will continue to put WA jobs first.”

Kerrin McEvoy rides Skyhook to victory in the listed Rosebud at Rosehill last year. Getty Images Payne, the patriarch of one of Australian racing’s most famous families, died this week at the age of 90 after a short illness. A former jumps jockey and trainer, Payne raised 10 children, eight of whom became jockeys, including pioneering Melbourne Cup winner, Michelle. McEvoy and Payne’s daughter, Cathy, have been together for almost 30 years, and he was among those to pay tribute.

“He’s down as 90, but I think he’s officially 93,” McEvoy said. “But a great innings, a great family man, great man, and he just loved his racing. Paddy Payne, father of 2015 Melbourne Cup winning jockey Michelle Payne at his family home where he raised his 10 children in Miners Rest. Jesse Marlow “He used to actually follow me as well as plenty of other family members. His kids had horses running left, right, and centre, with Paddy, Michelle and Andrew. He was always keen on how you were going, and gave you a shout if you had a winner. “He had a great time as a trainer himself and he was actually a jumps jockey before that. He rode plenty of winners and he would tell plenty of good stories about racing back in the day.

“He lived a good life. He’ll be sorely missed, but some great memories had with him along the way for all the kids and extended family.” McEvoy has excellent chances across the four features at Rosehill on Saturday, although trainer Chris Waller indicated Lady Shenandoah ($5.50) may be saved for another week after drawing wide as topweight in the group 2 Sheraco Stakes (1200m). Gerald Ryan and Sterling Alexiou-trained Skyhook, a $2.90 favourite for the group 2 Theo Marks Stakes (1300m), also has a wide gate. McEvoy had success taking Skyhook to the front from an outside barrier last time out in the group 3 Gunsynd Classic (1600m) on heavy going at Eagle Farm in June, but he was cautious of a repeat strategy first-up on Saturday. “He’s versatile, but I’ll have a sit down and chat with Gerald and Sterling,” he said.

“I don’t want a sizzling first run back, so we’ll see what it looks like in regards to where we ride him and whatnot. Kuniko Limited’s phase two diamond drilling campaign at its Silica Hill prospect in New South Wales has hit promising visual sulphides in several holes for the program, potentially extending the mineralised system by an extra 100 metres in depth. The company has now punched out 1324m of drilling in its ongoing program at Silica Hill, part of its broader Commonwealth gold-silver project in the fabled Lachlan Fold Belt. The latest holes have provided compelling evidence that the system continues to grow, with one hole intersecting a broad 70m-wide zone of sulphides and visually impressive veins up to half a metre thick. A diamond drill rig on site at Kuniko’s Silica Hill prospect in NSW. The company says its latest and fifth hole has also lit up with multiple visually prominent sulphide veins up to 50cm thick as it steps out to test the interpreted “Northern Lode” of the dual-loded Silica at depth. Kuniko’s latest drilling is building on the success of its recent phase one campaign, which delivered a spectacular intercept of 0.5m grading 20,603 grams per tonne (g/t) silver and 27g/t gold. That bonanza hit provided the impetus for the current systematic step-out program as the company looks to understand the major controls of its high-grade polymetallic system.

‘We have systematically stepped out from the known mineralisation and are seeing encouraging sulphide development.’ Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire Management says phase two drilling has now outlined two distinct mineralised lodes at Silica – a Northern Lode and a Southern Lode. Recent drilling has focused on thickening the Southern Lode, while also delivering a significant step-out hit that has extended the Northern Lode at depth. The company believes the project’s upside extends well beyond the known mineralisation. A recently completed geophysical review identified a prominent gravity-low feature associated with the existing mineralised system that continues for more than 500m to the south-east into largely untested ground. The anomaly suggests Silica could be part of a much larger district-scale mineralised system. Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire said: “Phase two drilling continues to build our confidence in the scale and continuity of the Silica Hill mineralised system. With 1324m now drilled, we have systematically stepped out from the known mineralisation and are seeing encouraging sulphide development across a significantly expanded footprint.“ The Commonwealth project sits 100 kilometres north of Orange in what is considered elephant country for mineral explorers. After drilling is complete and all outstanding assays are received, Kuniko plans to deliver an upgraded mineral resource estimate for the project in December, incorporating results from its phase one and two programs. With a string of visual sulphide hits from the drill bit in a proven mineral province, Kuniko looks to be steadily unravelling the scale of the Silica system. title: Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsBonds Opinion Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 10, 2026 — 12:12pm

September 10, 2026 — 12:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street brought “America’s top bond salesman” down a peg on Wednesday, reminding Donald Trump’s Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that not even the US government can fight the bond market. Bessent, who has claimed that title, last month announced plans for the US government to buy back $US2 billion ($2.8 billion) of longer-dated bonds. He subsequently doubled the target to $US4 billion and then, on Wednesday, raised the buyback, which is planned to happen on Thursday US time, to “up to $US6 billion”. If the increase was supposed to impress the market and depress bond yields, it failed. Scott Bessent at the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas on Wednesday. Bloomberg The yield on the benchmark 10-year bonds jumped from 4.79 per cent to 4.85 per cent. Apart from a brief moment in 2023, when the yield on the bonds almost hit 5 per cent, that’s the highest yield since 2007, before the global financial crisis.

Advertisement

Bessent’s buybacks are, he has said, designed to increase liquidity at the less liquid end of the market. He’s also claimed the surge in bond yields this year – which started the same day that the Trump administration and Israel launched their attack on Iran – doesn’t “reflect the underlying fundamentals of the market”. The yield on the 10-year bonds was 3.94 per cent on February 27, the eve of the attacks. The unpleasant reality for Bessent is that the rising yields in the market (two-year yields have jumped from 3.38 per cent on February 27 to 4.43 per cent and 30-year yields from 4.61 per cent to 5.29 per cent) in fact do reflect the fundamentals. It’s not just the war in the Middle East and its impact on energy prices and America’s inflation rate that, at 3.4 per cent, remains well above the US Federal Reserve Board’s 2 per cent target.

Advertisement

As the year has progressed, bond investors have become increasingly focused on the actual underlying fundamentals: US government deficits and debt that have blown out at an accelerating rate. The deficit is about 6 per cent of GDP, and gross government debt just passed $US40 trillion within a $US32.5 trillion economy. The ‘knife to a gunfight’ analogy doesn’t come anywhere close to capturing the futility of Bessent’s efforts to manipulate the market. The market knows that America is on an unsustainable fiscal trajectory, and has begun pricing in that risk. The problem for Bessent is that the interest costs on that debt, already more than $US1 trillion and the third-largest expenditure item in the government’s budget behind social security and Medicare, are rising rapidly.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

US politics Alarms flashing red as Trump takes US debt to level almost beyond comprehension Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent Every time those longer-dated 10- and 30-year bonds, which were issued within a lower-rate environment, mature and have to be refinanced, they attract a higher interest rate and drive the overall interest cost to the government higher. That increased cost of “old” debt is occurring even as the Trump administration has added new debt, increasing the total amount of debt on issue by about $US4 trillion since Trump regained office last year. Bessent’s attempt to cap yields via the buybacks might, at best, influence a day or two’s trading, but is destined to fail. His buybacks, even if he were to significantly increase their size, are inconsequential when set against the scale of a $US32 trillion market that trades $US1 trillion a day. The “knife to a gunfight” analogy doesn’t come anywhere close to capturing the futility of Bessent’s efforts to manipulate the market.

Advertisement

His intervention to try to prop up the Japanese yen might be more successful, but only because the fundamentals in Japan are shifting, with its bond yields, previously suppressed by decades of the Bank of Japan’s raft of unconventional monetary policies, rising. The modest US involvement in a large-scale BoJ yen-buying splurge was also motivated by Bessent’s efforts to protect the US market, with fears that Japan might have to offload its vast US bondholding to fund its defence of its currency, adding to the pressure for higher US yields. Similarly, Bessent’s support for the Genius Act – which would provide the first legislative and regulatory framework for the issuance of stablecoins, and create a large new source of buying for US bonds – can be viewed in the context of his efforts to suppress the upwards trend in US yields, as could his relaxation of some big bank capital regulations. What’s developing in the bond market could be, and has been, regarded as a normalisation of US yields after nearly two decades of abnormal monetary policies. Yields have been far higher in the past – they were above 5 per cent leading into the global financial crisis – without it threatening US economic growth or corporate stability.

Advertisement

However, the difference between then and now is what happened in the aftermath of the financial crisis to the economic settings of not just the US, but most of the developed countries. To stave off deflation, and even a depression, governments embraced aggressive fiscal stimulus and their central banks, borrowing from Japan, embarked on unconventional monetary policies. Quantitative easing – central bank buying of bonds and mortgages to suppress interest rates – and other measures to control yield curves were widespread. The bond market could respond and take matters into its own hands if Trump’s appointed chair Kevin Warsh doesn’t follow his recent hawkish words with action. AP The yields on government debt were driven down to near or even below zero – investors were, in fact, paying some central banks to keep their funds safe – which made the build-up in government debt near costless. The Fed, and its peers, left those novel monetary policies in place for the best part of a decade. The Fed didn’t start its “quantitative tightening” – the running down of the piles of bonds and mortgages it had acquired – until 2017.

Advertisement

Until the pandemic, there were negligible inflation rates in the developed economies (economists were debating how to increase inflation), so interest rates remained low, encouraging debt-issuance and debt-driven investment strategies. Sharemarkets boomed and non-banks – hedge funds and private equity – and ordinary investors made effectively riskless gains on their leveraged trades. The pandemic saw central banks again slash interest rates and governments open the debt spigots wide. Once the worst of the pandemic was over, and the disruptions to global supply chains ignited inflation rates, the central bankers began reversing course, but governments kept expanding their balance sheets in what was still a low-rate environment. That’s why the “normalisation” of bond yields towards historic levels is a threat to US and other economies’ stability. Today’s normal doesn’t look like the pre-financial crisis past.

Advertisement

In 2007, the US had about $US9 trillion of debt in a $US15 trillion economy. Today, it has $US40 trillion debt in a $US32.5 trillion economy. On the International Monetary Fund’s numbers, global government debt in 2007 was about 44 per cent of global GDP; today it’s 94 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Bonds The world is in a debt spiral and alarm signals are going off Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Next week, the Fed’s Open Market Committee meets, with the benefit of inflation data that will be available later this week, to decide whether to raise the Fed’s policy rate. An increase might only validate what’s already occurred within the market, but it might also shift the yield curve up a notch. While continued Fed inaction might be rationalised, the bond market could respond and take matters into its own hands if Trump’s appointed chair Kevin Warsh doesn’t follow his recent hawkish words with action. An increase in the federal funds rate (the equivalent of the Reserve Bank’s cash rate) would infuriate Trump and, more particularly, have Warsh and Bessent’s policies not just diverging, but colliding.

Advertisement

If there is a conflict between Warsh’s policies and Bessent’s, the Fed, with the support of the bond market, would inevitably prevail. Even without the Fed’s encouragement, the bond market “vigilantes”, having emerged from almost two decades of relative dormancy in response to the explosive growth of US debt and deficits, will determine the future of US rates. Bessent might boast that “I am the house now” while warning traders not to bet against the yen because, he says, he has “asymmetric” information about what the BoJ and Japanese government plan to do. With Japan gradually moving in a direction that investors advocate and support, he might not be challenged on that assertion. In America, however, his inside information means little because the rising tides of deficits and debt and a rediscovered awareness, by bond investors at least, of the need to price for risk will overwhelm any attempts by the US Treasury to game the market.
