title: ‘Who blinks first’: Government and rowing at odds over 2032 venue

NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics ‘Who blinks first’: Government and rowing at odds over 2032 venue Cameron Atfield September 10, 2026 — 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Queensland premier and his deputy have made a public show of force in Rockhampton to insist the Fitzroy River will host rowing events in 2032, after the sport’s world governing body cast doubt on its suitability to host Olympic competition. International rowing federations expressed scepticism of the plan during the World Rowing congress last week, which led to president Jean-Christophe Rolland to concede the governing body held concerns about the proposed venue. Standing near the banks of the Fitzroy River, Premier David Crisafulli said course testing was ongoing and he was confident it would get the “right result” for Olympic competition in 2032. All smiles: Premier David Crisafulli posted this image on social media in a public show of support for the Rockhampton Olympic rowing venue. David Crisafulli “Every so-called impediment that’s been put up has been dismissed by the people who live it and breathe and can understand it best,” he said.

Advertisement

“This is the last hurrah of people trying to find ways to, quite frankly, discredit something that makes a hell of a lot of sense, and we’re not for turning on this.” Crisafulli said Olympic rowing would be held in Rockhampton, “no ifs, no buts” – but there was a “but”. As QRowunion chairman Gary Merritt pointed out, the determination of whether the Fitzroy River was suitable for Olympic competition remained in the hands of World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee. “It is a case of who’s going to blink first,” Merritt said.

Advertisement

Referring to the City of Moreton Bay’s proposal for a purpose-built venue at an old quarry in Lawnton, Merritt said there was a “cheaper, better option” that would give more rowers a real legacy from the Olympic Games. “We’re going to spend all this money on a course in Rocky and, when the Olympics are over, there’s 150 people there who will use it – it’s not like we can take all of our big regattas up to Rocky. It’s just not going to happen,” he said. “It’s just going to be a huge white elephant and, in years to come, people are going to go, ‘What a waste of money that was.’” World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland has expressed concern about the course. Sebastian Kahnert/Getty Images But Merritt conceded rowing had missed the boat in not being able to present a fully formed proposal for the Moreton Bay facility in time for the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority’s 100-day review.

Advertisement

“We have to take some responsibility,” he said. “But having owned up to the fact that we didn’t have everything prepared as we should have, we’re now at a stage where we’re saying we can rescue the situation, but there’s just been no openness or any attempt to scrutinise what’s possible.” The proposed flatwater centre at Lawnton, with the Moreton Bay Indoor Sports Centre in the background. City of Moreton Bay If GIICA considered the Moreton Bay site, it did not rate a mention in its review. Rockhampton was considered, but GIICA rejected it as an option due to its “insufficient space for field of play and warm-up, inadequate onshore space and access road upgrade requirements, as well as limited accommodation options for athletes and officials”.

Advertisement

On the accommodation question, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said Olympic rowing would be the catalyst for more supply in the central Queensland city. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Rocky rowing critics think they’re ‘too good for regional Queensland’: premier “With the accommodation, that’s a temporary overlay for the athletes’ village to house 1200 athletes – we’re in the process of working that out with [the Brisbane 2032 Organising Committee] and also GIICA,” he said. “We’re looking also at land activation programs, which is state-owned land, and how we can get houses on it, [and] hotel opportunities. “There’s a need for hotels right across regional Queensland – so many people are wanting to move and visit regional Queensland, so we need all that.”

Advertisement

Arguments against Rockhampton have ranged from its distance from the main Olympic hub in Brisbane, to an unfair field of play, and even the potential for crocodiles. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics ‘Out of his depth’: Rowers escalate Rocky revolt against Bleijie In Rowing Queensland’s safety management plan for this month’s Queensland Schools’ Championship Regatta on the river, there are contingencies for crocodile sightings. “Upon receiving a ‘Crocodile Crocodile Crocodile’ call the following steps are to be carried out as quickly as possible,” the plans says. “Establish the nature of the emergency; Inform regatta control of sighting and location; Racing to be suspended; Competitors instructed to return to the bank; Officials ensure all boats are removed from the water.”

Ukraine and Moldova have played down claims from Norway's prime minister that a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was almost hit by a drone as it flew to Oslo.

Jonas Gahr Støre told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK on Thursday AEST that Zelenskyy's plane was "almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova".

"It was an alert in Moldova when a Russian (drone) entered Moldovan and Romanian airspace," the source told the Agence France-Presse news agency (AFP).

"I think more than anything else, it's two people that hate each other."

title: The countries showing Australia a way out of its 'miserable' classroom situation
text:
Heightened classroom disruption, gender divides, dwindling reading and maths scores — a major global student performance report shows Australian schools are continuing to slide backwards on key measures.

Every three years, the global Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) measures student literacy in mathematics, reading, science and computational problem-solving.

The 2025 edition, which tested 15-year-olds from 91 OECD countries and economies, also measured the effects of gender divides, differences between high and low socio-economic status, and the impacts of technology and classroom disruption.

In the latest report, released on Tuesday, Australia's scores continued a 20-year decline, with maths and reading at Australia's lowest since testing began in 2000.

But Pasi Sahlberg, a Finnish education expert, author and professor at the University of Melbourne, says reports focusing on issues with the Australian school system were missing the big picture.

"The headline is that we have all-time-low results. I think it's absolutely astonishing that our mainstream media are saying this. The truth is every country in the OECD is showing all-time-low results in everything. Very few countries were able to improve their results in 2025," Sahlberg told SBS News.

Australia's scores are on a 20-year decline, but that isn't the full story. Source: SBS News

In the global ranking, Australia moved up one place in reading to 11th, maintained its 17th place in maths, and fell one place in science to 11th. In the computational problem solving category, introduced in 2025, Australia ranked 8th globally. Australia's scores were well above the OECD average in all four key tests.

On Wednesday, in light of the results, federal Education Minister Jason Clare announced new reforms in reading, mathematics and science. He pointed to England's success — the country jumped three places in reading to reach the top 10, four places in maths to 10th place and seven places in science to rank at 8th in the 2025 PISA report — to illustrate a need for various reforms. This includes a focus on phonics, which is a method of teaching reading and writing that uses the sounds of spoken language, changes to the maths curriculum, and reforms to screen time.

"The UK results are impressive. It’s also hard-earned. It’s something almost 20 years in the making," Clare said in a statement.

He said that Australian schools that have been following English methods for a while are showing improvements but he wants a broader roll-out.

There has been a general decline in literacy across all OECD countries. Source: SBS News

'We are all in this miserable situation together'

But Sahlberg said Clare's reforms were the wrong response.

"We need to look beyond these rankings, because this data is also showing us a very alarming situation in Australia and many other countries when it comes to how young people experience learning in school."

Sahlberg said the issues affecting children's learning also occurred outside the classroom: parents are reading less and have less interest or engagement with their children's schooling.

The PISA report, which showed that 75 per cent of students in Australia reported that their parents or guardians asked them, at least once per week, what they did at school, down from 81 per cent in 2022.

"England, Canada, USA, all the others, we are all in this miserable situation together," when it comes to a decline in a positive culture around reading, he said.

What are countries with the highest scores doing that Australia isn't?

In the Asia-Pacific region, several Chinese regions, Singapore, Taiwan (which participates in PISA under the name Chinese Taipei), Macao and Japan took the top five PISA spots across mathematics, reading, science and computational problem-solving.

While Singapore and Japan's scores decreased slightly from the previous PISA ranking, Taiwan, China and Macao all saw slight increases in their scores, outliers across most participating OECD countries.

Australia's mathematics score remained steady in 2025. Source: SBS News

For Therese Keane, digital learning expert and professor in STEM Education in the School of Education at La Trobe University, the secret to Singapore's success was in its handling of technology in the classroom.

"Singapore is a great example of combining high technology with clear learning guidance, with subject-specific digital learning guidance in schools," she told SBS News.

Keane said that technology was ushered into Australian classrooms hastily during former prime minister Kevin Rudd's digital education revolution program. She said the quick move left the technology ubiquitous, without proper guidelines for use.

"Technology is important in the classroom, but it needs to be used with intention and guidelines," Keane said.

"I think we've got to be very careful that we don't throw the baby out with the bath water in terms of technology and AI because when you look at countries like Singapore, Estonia, the regions of China, PISA shows that the technologies do not automatically undermine the learning."

Estonia, a country with a strong focus on tech, nonetheless ranks highly in reading literacy. Source: SBS News

She said the difference is that technology is embedded within a strong system of teaching, curriculum, expectations and classroom management.

"These high performing countries that we're seeing, they're not anti-technology. And I want the message to be that they're much more willing to draw a hard line between, say, learning technology and personal technology."

But there are big cultural and structural differences at play, too. Sahlberg, who has worked in schools across Singapore, Japan and China, said that high PISA scores seen in those countries come at a "huge" social cost.

READ MORE Could AI in classrooms stop children falling behind at school?

"In these countries, about 80 to 100 per cent of kids go to school after daily school."

"They have their private lessons every evening, and then they go to school on Saturdays and often Sundays as well — this comes with a huge human cost, and social cost."

Sahlberg said that if Australia wanted to do something similar to those high-performing countries, then a question to ask would be, "how many parents would like to do that to their own children?"

Australia ranked equal tenth with New Zealand for science literacy. Source: SBS News

But, he said, the solution to Australia's problem was clear.

"We don't need to go to Singapore or England or Shanghai to see what they do; we have the solution in this country.

"Our politicians and system leaders should redesign the school architecture: We have 24 jurisdictions, and they don't share their best practices; they don't tell others what works in their systems because they are competing.

The countries and economies topping the PISA rankings all have a more centralised learning curriculum, but in Australia, there are vast differences between our state, Catholic and independent schools. Salhberg says supporting the current "highly competitive, fragmented, siloed education system that is incapable of learning from itself" was a waste of learning opportunities.

"How can we release this potential and good practice that we have in this country?" he asked.

"This is the lesson we should take from PISA."

title: Winner of Alone Season 4 plans to donate some of their $250,000 prize to a competitor
text:
in brief Former Navy chef Trent Fenton survived 52 freezing days to win Alone Australia season four.

Now back home, he plans to pay off his mortgage and support fellow competitors.

"It was a feeling that I'll cherish for the rest of my life."

Alone Australia season four has reached its icy conclusion with one man left standing in Finland's frozen north: Trent Fenton.

The 40-year-old former Navy chef told SBS News in his first post-show interview that re-watching the moment his wife Em tapped him on the shoulder to reveal he had made it still gets him.

"I started even choking up a little bit, which was weird because I'm not that kind of guy normally," Fenton said.

"That's why people love Alone. It's just pure emotion."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Season four of the hit survivalist show took participants away from Oceania and into the wilds of Sápmi, deep within the Arctic Circle. Dropped along the shore of lake Rahajärvi, they had to battle sub-zero temperatures, extreme calorie deficits, and total isolation for a chance to win $250,000.

Father-of-three Fenton spent 52 days alone, outlasting nine other contenders — who either gave up or were deemed medically unable to continue — but said he is "no amazing survivalist".

Asked what he plans to do with the prize, he says he plans to donate part of it to causes championed by some of his competitors and pay down his mortgage.

The final episode of the season saw the other remaining finalists — 57-year-old farmer Clint and 24-year-old permaculture educator Jasper — pushed to their limits.

After spending a night spent throwing up, Clint called time on his 48th day in the wilderness, saying, "there are things in life worth more than money — like health, love, companionship, friends and family".

"When you haven’t got them, you realise just how important they are.”

Just a day later, Jasper was medically extracted after an infection in his hand was found to be spreading. He said he was leaving the show "a new person" after being challenged in the extreme.

"These 48 days have been some of the best of my life," Jasper said. "I’m proud of how far I pushed myself and feel at peace knowing I’ve done the experience justice."

Perspective the key to survival

As a child, Fenton said he would "get into a bit of strife", which prompted his father to relocate the family from Hobart to the Tasmanian Midlands where he could "get my nose clean".

"Mate, I've never looked back. I love everything about the bush and hunting and fishing," he said. "It was really my element out there."

The well-honed skills needed to sustain himself on whatever he could catch or forage were backed by a "bucketload of resilience", which Fenton said he developed in the Navy.

Ten survivalists ventured into the remote Arctic wilderness of Sápmi, Finland, for Alone Australia season four. Credit: SBS

"I joined the Navy not knowing that I suffered severe seasickness," he said. "After four years throwing my guts up, I thought, 'If you can push through something like that, it puts you in good stead for most things that you're going to run into'."

Still, Fenton said he entered the competition with the mentality that it would be "the adventure of a lifetime" and that, even if he faced starvation, as many contestants do, he was always in the "privileged" position to be able to escape it — unlike many around the world, particularly those in Gaza.

All about the trout

The strategy which saw him take home $250,000 in prize money relied on bringing in as many fish as he could. While Finland was "a bit colder than good old Tassie", Fenton said as long as he had access to fish, he believed he would have a solid chance.

His commitment to fishing meant that, unusually for a contestant on Alone — which often sees people go for weeks without a solid meal — Fenton rarely struggled for food.

"One of the producers actually said to me, 'Trent, I've seen no one in the existence of Alone Australia put in as much time fishing or making stuff to fish as you did'," he said.

Temperatures in northern Finland can reach as low as negative 30C, with snow covering the ground from October through to April. Credit: SBS

Reliance on fishing, however, meant that the day he lost a prized, handmade lure which had secured him over 30 fish was a real blow.

"I was devastated," he said. "If you watch the last episode ... I had a full dummy spit, and I threw my rod, and I was swearing."

"If someone said to me, 'Mate, you give me your car at home and I'll give that lure back to you', I would have done it in a heartbeat."

'Dark days' in the final stretch

Even with his well-stocked bag of dried fish, Fenton said not knowing whether his competitors also had food meant never quite feeling secure and constantly wondering if he had enough to outlast them.

The "dark days" came just before his seven-week-plus finish when the lake began to freeze but the ice wasn't thick enough to walk on.

"I couldn't spear fish ... I couldn't go and forage any berries or mushrooms ... what do I actually do?" Fenton said. "I just thought, 'I don't really want to be here, this is rubbish, I'm just bored, I can't do anything'."

Little did he know, he was just hours away from seeing his wife again, something that Fenton said was challenging to re-adjust to.

"I wasn't ready to go home. I hadn't mentally prepared or even started checking out for that," he said.

"A couple of days after getting taken off the land, some weird things go through your mind, and I struggled to come to terms with a lot of them."

Memories and money

Now that he's back in his regular life, Fenton said he plans to pay off the mortgage, invest money for his children to use later in life, and start "creating memories" with his family.

He also plans to donate some of his winnings to fellow competitor and ex-serviceman Dylan Hyatt-Jacobson, who opened up about his family's struggles with IVF treatment during his time on the show.

Ultramarathon runner Sia Kindberg, who tapped out in episode six due to frostbite, is raising money for survivors of slavery, human trafficking, and abuse with a Sydney to Melbourne run in October. Fenton said he will be donating to her cause as well.

As the temperatures dropped, the fish Fenton relied on moved into deeper, warmer water, where he was unable to follow them across the thin ice. Credit: SBS

Incredibly, after 52 days, the Alone Australia season four winner said he may not be done just yet — and is keen to find out exactly where his breaking point is.

"All the other competitors ... they could either see that they were medically unfit, or they were literally physically checked out; they know where their breaking point is. Whereas I kind of didn't experience that," Fenton said.

"Hopefully there's another time where there's another season of Alone with all the winners or something like that.

"That would be another amazing experience just to try and have another crack."

title: How an NFL match in Melbourne came to be, and its historic links
text:
In brief The NFL will stage its first regular-season game in Australia, with the 49ers facing the Rams at the MCG.

The multi-year NFL deal, secured amid stiff interstate competition, has Melbourne preparing to host up to 100,000 fans.

Anticipation is building ahead of the NFL's big Australian debut.

The San Francisco 49ers take on the Los Angeles Rams at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on Friday morning in what will be the league's first regular-season game in Australia, and just the second game overall of the 2026 season.

The match kicks off on Friday at 10.35am and is geared around the Thursday night TV audience in the US. Kick-off time will be 5.35pm on the US West Coast and 8.35pm on the East Coast.

How did the NFL land in Victoria?

The NFL has a four-year contract with Victoria to host at least two games in Melbourne, with an option for a third, and is part of the NFL’s International Series, which started in 2007 at London's Wembley Stadium.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The Victorian government beat out serious bids from both NSW and Western Australia to host these games, and is thought to be paying the NFL about $15 million per game.

How often does the NFL play outside the US?

The match at the MCG will be one of nine international matches scheduled this season — including matches in Paris, Rio de Janeiro, Munich, Madrid, and London. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell has expressed interest in having every team play once in a foreign market each season.

Games have also been staged in Germany, Brazil, Mexico and Canada before.

While exhibition games between NFL teams have been played beyond US borders since 1969, some countries, like England, took time to build a following, while others, like Mexico, embraced it immediately.

In fact, the largest crowd in NFL history is 112,376 at the Azteca Stadium in Mexico City in 1994 when the Houston Oilers beat the Dallas Cowboys.

Other stadiums have also hosted NFL regular-season games outside the United States, including the Bernabéu in Madrid, Croke Park in Dublin, Twickenham in London, plus stadiums in Berlin, Munich, Frankfurt and São Paulo in Brazil.

The NFL has ramped up international efforts in recent times by inviting teams to apply for international marketing rights for various countries.

Are both the teams in Australia already?

As of Wednesday afternoon, only one of the two teams playing on Friday — the San Francisco 49ers — has arrived in Australia.

"This has been such a cool experience," said 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey.

"There were question marks when we heard we were playing in Australia. Since we got here, it has been so cool. The people are unbelievable, the food's incredible, the coffee is great. The atmosphere, you can already feel it, it's been so much fun and we are super fired up we're here."

Four teams have been given the rights to Australia and New Zealand — the Los Angeles Rams, Philadelphia Eagles, Las Vegas Raiders, and the reigning Super Bowl champions, the Seattle Seahawks.

Therein lies one of the ironies of this week.

The Rams are one of Australia's designated teams — but they're not here until 24 hours before the game, electing to try to stay on US time to avoid jet lag — a fly-in, fly-out mission.

San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan says the team has acclimatised to the time difference after a 16-hour flight from the US. Source: AAP / Joel Carrett

The 49ers players have been taking in some of the sights and sounds of Melbourne, and winning a lot of local hearts in the process. Already one of the NFL's more popular teams, it's now even more likely there will be more 49ers fans than Rams fans among the expected 100,000 fans at the MCG on Friday.

Ironically, 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan was perhaps the loudest complainer when this game was scheduled earlier this year.

“Nothing against (Melbourne). It looks awesome. People seem really cool. Makes me want to come back and visit with my family," Shanahan told reporters.

"But we have 17 games. We play once a week, so we are all about business right now ... My message to the players was to enjoy their one day off, get hydrated and get used to the time difference. And we have done that."

A historical precedent

It's not the first time two US teams will take to the hallowed ground of the MCG — the first American football match played there was in 1908, between sailors of the USS Minnesota and the USS Kentucky.

In 1925, the US sent a 57-warship armada for a friendly visit to Australia and New Zealand, a post-war exercise in geopolitical and public relations designed to boost sailor morale while also building Pacific alliances in the face of growing Japanese aggression.

Forty-three of those ships would arrive in Melbourne to great public interest.

Records show that US sailors held boxing matches and played baseball at the MCG against some of the best Australian cricketers of the day. But it was a gridiron match between US sailors from the USS Trenton and USS Pennsylvania that caught Melbourne's attention.

At a muddy Punt Road Oval, a stone's throw from the MCG, sailors from the Pennsylvania beat the sailors from the Trenton in front of 3,000 people in a match that, according to the Royal Historical Society of Victoria, included VFL footballers.

In 1999, the Denver Broncos and San Diego Chargers played a pre-season exhibition match in Sydney in 1999. The match was played at Stadium Australia in Homebush in front of almost 74,000 fans. In the heart of rugby league country, its American mutation drew curiosity but failed to satisfy. The New York Times' John Shaw reported at the time that the crowd was "about 20,000 smaller" than the NFL had hoped for. Shaw reported that "canned applause was frequently blasted across the stadium when the audience was slow to cheer".

How to watch San Francisco 49ers vs Los Angeles Rams in Australia?

Kick off is at 10.35am for the eastern states and territories, 10.05am in SA and the NT, and 8.35am in WA.

Australians will be able to watch the match on Fox Sports and Kayo via a subscription, or on free-to-air on Seven or 7Plus. Coverage starts at 10am.

title: 'Absolute nightmare': Mass flight cancellations in the UK prompt calls for dismissals
text:
in brief A total of 1,055 flights to and from UK airports had been axed by 8pm (5am AEST) .

Ryanair COO Neal McMahon repeated his calls for NATS chief executive Martin Rolfe to be fired.

Consumer chaos has descended on the UK's busiest airports as an air traffic glitch causes major disruptions, prompting calls to fire the head of the air traffic control service.

Almost 1,100 flights to and from UK airports were cancelled Tuesday, due to what the country's air traffic control service called a technical issue, in this latest error.

A total of 1,055 flights to and from British airports had been axed by 8pm (5am AEST) according to the aircraft tracking website FlightRadar24.

"Recovery from today's system issue has taken longer than we had hoped," Britain's air traffic control service, known as NATS, said on social media.

"Our system issue is now resolved, we are operating normally and working as hard as possible to clear the backlog of flights," it noted, adding "this is hugely frustrating and apologise unreservedly".

Tuesday's issues follow a technical glitch in July last year that saw scores of flights to and from the UK cancelled and which prompted anger from airline chiefs.

Britain saw its worst air systems failure in years in 2023, with more than 700,000 passengers affected after hundreds of flights were delayed or cancelled.

'Absolute nightmare'

Heathrow Airport, Britain's largest and busiest airport, in west London, confirmed it was among those affected on Tuesday, along with Gatwick to the south of the UK capital.

Arsenal, due to play Napoli in the Champions League on Wednesday in the southern Italian city, were forced to cancel a press conference ahead of the match after the team's flight was delayed.

title: The taboo wealth tax debate experts say Australia can no longer ignore
text:
in brief Rising intergenerational wealth transfers are widening Australia's economic divide by rewarding inherited capital over earned wages.

Experts argue that unaddressed untaxed wealth threatens retirement security and demands urgent structural tax reform.

Australia faces a "tsunami" of retirees unable to support themselves if it doesn't address the growing issue of untaxed intergenerational wealth transfer, advocates warn.

New research from the Australian Institute of Family Studies (AIFS) released on Wednesday shows that intergenerational financial support — flowing from older, wealthy family members to younger ones — is increasingly driving inequality.

The report found that Australians receiving inheritance grew from 4.8 per cent to 7.2 per cent between 2001 and 2018 while the proportion receiving financial gifts grew from 10.5 per cent to 15. 8 per cent over the same period.

The timing of such financial aid has a major impact, the report emphasises, with earlier assistance shaping opportunities at critical life stages. Inheritance, while typically larger, often comes after decisions around housing have been made.

"Not all families have the same capacity to provide assistance," Dr Jody Hughes, head of families and society at the AIFS said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Understanding who can access these forms of support, and who misses out, is important for understanding broader patterns of wellbeing, financial security and inequality both between and within generations."

The new data comes as comparison site Finder revealed that 30 per cent of homeowners in Australia received financial support from family to buy their homes. Home loans expert Richard Witten noted that the "bank of mum and dad has become a major player" in the property market.

Christian charitable community services network Anglicare has been campaigning on tax reform to address inequality, with its own data finding the baby boomer generation is set to pass on roughly $5.4 trillion to their families — much of it untaxed.

Kasy Chambers, executive director of Anglicare, told SBS News that Australia's unusual lack of inheritance tax and its generous superannuation concessions allows wealth to "build and build".

"We're about to see the biggest wealth transfer ever in human history," she said. "That will concentrate wealth, which doesn't really do anybody any good because it takes it out of tax systems, it puts it in the hands of a very small amount, and it makes running any kind of government services ... very, very difficult."

Chambers noted Anglicare is seeing a rise in people using its services as precarity climbs the income ladder, driving more people to food banks.

"Normal is not enough," she notes, explaining that families on median incomes are increasingly struggling to afford the basics.

Is a death tax the answer?

In May, the government came under fire as its reforms to trusts were branded a "death tax" by the Opposition.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers introduced changes in the budget to discretionary trusts, imposing a minimum 30 per cent tax rate from 2028 and making their use by families to distribute income to beneficiaries less attractive, and denied the proposal was a death tax.

Australia abolished its inheritance tax in 1979, making it an outlier in developed nations, most of which have some form of duty owed on capital and assets transferred to family members.

Chambers supported the government's reforms to superannuation and capital gains tax but said Labor should go further.

"It's unpopular, but when you model what happens when people that have wealth simply pass all of it on, it very quickly ends up very, very concentrated," she said.

Other experts aren't so sure, with Tax and Transfer Policy Institute Director, Professor Robert Breunig, telling SBS News that such taxes could sound good in theory but fail in practice.

Upper-middle class individuals who die unexpectedly tend to shoulder the greatest burden of inheritance taxes, as "really wealthy" individuals frequently make adjustments to avoid paying them, he said.

Labor's tax reforms primarily affect income tax while largely avoiding wealth accumulation, such as the value of property and inheritance, which the AIFS report notes is the primary driver of growing inequality.

Breunig notes that such inequality is not intergenerational — ie, between baby boomers and millennials — but a growing class one between those with wealthy families and those without.

The housing safety net

Parental support is not only helping young people buy homes, it is also widening the wealth gap, as financial support is more likely to go to those who are already homeowners, the report highlights.

Miriam and her partner, both in their 30s, told SBS News that they have been saving for a house deposit since before they got married over a decade ago. Currently, the couple is in the final stages of closing on their first home in Sydney's Baulkham Hills — a $1.4 million townhouse.

"We've been making sacrifices across the board," Miriam said. "We tried to not live closer to the city, so that we wouldn't be paying so much in rent just to make sure that we kept putting into our savings".

Even so, the couple said they would have been unable to afford the deposit or secure a loan without borrowing around 40 per cent of the value of the home from her partner's family.

"It means we'll be using most of our savings," she said. "We will be paying it back; it's just instead of paying a mortgage and interest, you're paying your family. That means sacrificing for the next few years, on a lot of things."

Without similar support, Miriam said many of her friends assume they will "have to rent" for the rest of their lives.

Chambers notes that "the whole aged care system is really built on an assumption that people will have their own home" by the time they retire.

Renting in retirement is "actually pretty grim," Anglicare modelling shows, with more people expected to enter aged care earlier as they simply run out of money.

"It actually is a bit of a tsunami that's going to hit the country if we don't address it in some way," she said.

Breunig, however, argues that while homeownership is down "a little bit" among younger Australians, people are still buying homes later in life. That demographic will also have benefited from having had superannuation for longer, so are likely to be better off in retirement, he said.

'Something' must be done

The bigger driver of wealth inequality is a tax system that doesn't account for the vast rise in property prices over the last 20 years, Breunig argued.

"[Growing inequality is a result of] our failure to tax the major vehicle in which people hold their wealth," he said.

Data varies, but around 40 per cent of total wealth in Australia is in owner-occupied housing. Breunig argues that, at some point, something will need to be done about it.

While he said a "death tax" is likely politically too toxic, he advocates for a broad-based land tax to "really tax the wealth people are holding in property".

The ACT is halfway through its 20-year plan to transition the territory toward this arrangement, although the federal government has repeatedly rejected calls for a national land tax.

Making the economic changes necessary to avoid runaway inequality is deeply unpopular, Chambers said, arguing a "loss of trust in governments and institutions" means people want more of their income.

"If we don't do something ... we're going to end up in a place that's not really very great for anyone," she said. "And it's not that far away; it'll be in a couple of generations."

title: 'No choice': Grim interest rate warning for borrowers as oil prices spike
text:
In brief Some banks are tipping a September rate rise amid higher-than-expected inflation.

RBA assistant governor Sarah Hunter said inflation is a "top priority right now".

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) might have to raise interest rates if inflation is higher than expected as oil prices surge back towards US$100 a barrel.

More attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz drove Brent crude above US$97 a barrel, which will seep into domestic petrol and diesel prices and broader cost pressures for businesses.

Russel Chesler, VanEck's head of investments and capital markets, expects oil prices to stay higher for longer.

"The continuing Middle East conflict is showing no signs of a resolution and that will leave the RBA with no choice but to increase rates at its meeting later this month," he said.

RBA assistant governor Sarah Hunter did little to downplay expectations the bank would lift interest rates again if inflation continued to exceed its forecasts.

Both headline and trimmed mean inflation came in above the RBA's forecasts in July.

Ongoing price pressures from the Middle East conflict have been taking their toll on businesses, particularly in manufacturing, construction and retail, NAB head of Australian economics Gareth Spence said.

Business conditions took a tumble in August, with profitability falling 10 points to the lowest level since the pandemic, NAB's monthly business survey showed on Tuesday.

How much businesses are able to pass through those costs to consumers will help determine how sticky inflation will remain going forward.

And it will depend on how willing households are to keep spending.

Confidence drops among mortgage borrowers

Expectations of more rate rises caused sentiment among home owners to collapse in September, the Westpac-Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index showed.

Confidence plummeted 14 per cent among mortgage holders in the month, compared to a 0.9 per cent fall among renters.

''Interest rate concerns had a clear negative impact on consumers with a mortgage," Westpac's head of Australian macro-forecasting Matthew Hassan said.

Overall, the consumer sentiment index declined 5.2 per cent to 84.4, as interest rate expectations climbed 7.3 per cent.

Despite economists forecasting the housing downturn to deepen as high interest rates combine with federal budget tax changes, only 32 per cent of consumers expected prices to decline over the next 12 months, with 42 per cent expecting a rise.

HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham expects nationwide house prices to fall 13 per cent peak to trough, which would be "the largest housing price correction in modern history".

Already, $34.1 billion has been wiped off Australian property values in the three months ended June, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.

The 0.3 per cent decline pales in comparison to the 12.3 per cent increase since the start of 2025.

title: Flights resume in Indonesia despite fresh volcanic eruptions
text:
In brief Jakarta's main airport has reopened following days of travel chaos triggered by a volcanic eruption.

The Anak Krakatau volcano erupted three more times on Tuesday morning.

Indonesia has reopened its main airport in Jakarta and four others that had been closed due to volcanic ash, although fresh eruptions on Tuesday raised the risk of further disruption.

Ash from the Anak Krakatau volcano, which sits halfway between Java and Sumatra islands, has blanketed Jakarta and some surrounding areas since its initial eruption late on Friday.

It led to the closure of eight airports for safety reasons, with more than 340,000 travellers impacted.

Soekarno-Hatta Airport, Jakarta's main airport, resumed operations on Tuesday after wind blew the ash away, transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi said in a statement, adding that authorities would check the airworthiness of 178 planes that were grounded there during the closure.

"Perhaps it'll take some little extra time to prepare the planes," Dudy said.

Traveller Alvin Pratama Putra, 31, who had arrived at Soekarno-Hatta on Sunday for a flight to South Korea for work, said his flight had now been rescheduled to Thursday.

"What can you do? It's nature. It's dangerous for the plane if you force it," he said, adding that he had been sleeping on a bench at the airport.

Four other airports, including a smaller one in Jakarta and another in the neighbouring city of Bandung, also reopened on Tuesday. Another airport had already reopened on Monday, while two remain closed.

Bayu Sutanto, secretary general of the Indonesia National Air Carriers Association (INACA), said the delays put strain on airlines' finances, with lost revenue from cancelled flights and higher operating expenses.

Bayu said airlines would have to incur various expenses such as extra fuel costs from route diversions, aircraft parking, or crew-related costs, adding that a delay of one plane at Soekarno-Hatta could affect the next three or four flights using the same aircraft.

Airlines could lose up to $1.5 million a day during such a disruption, Bayu said.

Fresh eruptions

Anak Krakatau erupted again three times on Tuesday morning, the local volcano monitoring agency said.

While smaller than the earlier eruptions, there was still potential for further flight disruption depending on ash height and wind direction.

"So far, the impact is not as big as the previous eruptions, but we'll continue to monitor," said Lana Saria, head of the geological agency.

Mount Anak Krakatau in the Java Strait has erupted several times since 2020. Source: EPA

The volcano is one of about 130 active volcanoes in Indonesia, which straddles the 'Pacific Ring of Fire', a highly seismically active zone where tectonic plates meet to produce numerous earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

Other volcanoes, including Mount Ibu and Ili Lewotolok, both on islands east of Java, also erupted on Tuesday.

Anak Krakatau, which means child of Krakatau, began emerging a century ago from the area previously occupied by Krakatau, then known as Krakatoa. The older volcano destroyed itself in mass eruptions in 1883, which killed more than 36,000 people after triggering a series of tsunamis.

title: Anthony Albanese says he's not trying to stop you from doomscrolling
text:
In brief Digital duty of care laws will compel social media companies to protect users from harmful content.

It will also offer Australians the option to opt out of seeing personally recommended content from social media algorithms.

Australian internet users will be given the choice to opt out of algorithmic recommendations under proposed social media reforms.

Draft laws setting up a digital duty of care were introduced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Tuesday.

As part of the measures, social media companies will need to provide tools for people to choose what they see in their online feeds, under a government initiative called My Feed, My Way.

Social media companies have been accused of creating addictive algorithms that keep people endlessly scrolling through recommended content. Advocates have called for a reversion to chronological feeds that show posts from friends and other accounts a user follows.

"This is not about giving government control. It's about giving people control. It's about putting choice back into the hands of Australians online," Albanese told reporters in Canberra.

"If people want to doom scroll, as you call it, that's fine, that's up to them," he said.

"But if people want to have a change, then this will provide them with the opportunity."

He pointed to global discussion over harms linked to social media, including at the United Nations.

"It's a debate that's taking place in countries all around the world, because of the sort of impact that we're seeing," he added, citing a rise in mental health issues and eating disorders as examples.

The reforms had drawn backlash from both the Coalition and Greens before being formally announced, with Opposition leader Angus Taylor suggesting it could be akin to censorship.

Meanwhile, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young called for the opt-out algorithm to be made the default setting.

'A global reckoning coming for big tech'

Under the draft laws, social media companies will also be required to protect people from harmful content online.

Harmful content will include the promotion of eating disorders, misogynistic content, pornography or content that glorifies crime.

Albanese said the legislation would empower the government to issue removal notices for 'nudify' apps and websites, which typically use artificial intelligence to create fake nude images of people without their consent.

Sharing that type of content — nonconsensual deepfake sexualised images — is already illegal in much of Australia, but developing the tools to do so isn't.

Companies could face fines of $100 million if they don't enact the duty of care.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said the duty of care would build on the world-leading ban on social media for under-16s Australia introduced last year.

"The digital duty of care is not about controlling adults online. It is about giving adults a choice," she said.

"Tech companies can still move fast, but they will no longer be allowed to break things because online harms have real-world consequences.

"There is a global reckoning coming for big tech."

It follows the government looking to pursue stronger penalties for social media companies as part of measures to bolster the under-16s ban.

Western Australia’s peak mining and energy body remains firm that the state should remain separate from a national gas reservation scheme after the federal government released the proposed legislation for consultation. The Domestic Gas Reservation Bill 2026 aims to establish Australia’s first national gas reservation policy to secure local supply for Australians and put downward pressure on domestic prices. Chamber of Minerals and Energy Western Australia chief executive Aaron Morey. Trevor Collens The scheme requires exporters to supply a portion of the gas they produce to the domestic market, with the initial proposal looking to reserve up to 20 per cent of gas exports. However, Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive Aaron Morey believes the current state government policy remains the best option for West Australians.

Advertisement

Under legislation set out by the state government two decades ago, WA gas exporters are currently required to provide a 15 per cent proportion of their exports to the domestic market – although that figure is set over the life of a project, not an annual designation, which remains a point of contention. Morey said WA had the balance right in its domestic scheme. “We remain absolutely certain that the best thing for Western Australia is for it not to be included in this scheme,” he said. “[The WA policy] is a scheme that has flexibility at its heart, and that has resulted in a set of outcomes that has worked for everyone.” Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King said under the proposed scheme, domestic supply obligations must be met in the same market as the export facility.

“An eastern exporter cannot meet their obligations by selling gas into the western market,” she said. “In a market that is well supplied, the domestic supply obligation can be reduced. For example, if the western market were found to be well supplied, it would be possible for discretion to be applied to reduce that obligation to zero.” King said WA’s scheme was about ensuring the state was well provided for in terms of gas for households, but also manufacturing and refining. “Different providers there provide different amounts of gas and that’s all agreed with the state government,” she said. “If the state government is satisfied with that because it’s their obligation, they’ve taken that obligation earlier than anyone else to make sure that their citizens and their industry is supplied with gas.”

However, Greenpeace Australia Pacific WA campaigns lead Geoff Bice said the gas industry had been getting away with “daylight robbery” in WA for years. title: Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsBonds Opinion Trump’s ‘top bond salesman’ is getting a reality check Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 10, 2026 — 12:12pm

September 10, 2026 — 12:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street brought “America’s top bond salesman” down a peg on Wednesday, reminding Donald Trump’s Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that not even the US government can fight the bond market. Bessent, who has claimed that title, last month announced plans for the US government to buy back $US2 billion ($2.8 billion) of longer-dated bonds. He subsequently doubled the target to $US4 billion and then, on Wednesday, raised the buyback, which is planned to happen on Thursday US time, to “up to $US6 billion”. If the increase was supposed to impress the market and depress bond yields, it failed. Scott Bessent at the Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas on Wednesday. Bloomberg The yield on the benchmark 10-year bonds jumped from 4.79 per cent to 4.85 per cent. Apart from a brief moment in 2023, when the yield on the bonds almost hit 5 per cent, that’s the highest yield since 2007, before the global financial crisis.

Advertisement

Bessent’s buybacks are, he has said, designed to increase liquidity at the less liquid end of the market. He’s also claimed the surge in bond yields this year – which started the same day that the Trump administration and Israel launched their attack on Iran – doesn’t “reflect the underlying fundamentals of the market”. The yield on the 10-year bonds was 3.94 per cent on February 27, the eve of the attacks. The unpleasant reality for Bessent is that the rising yields in the market (two-year yields have jumped from 3.38 per cent on February 27 to 4.43 per cent and 30-year yields from 4.61 per cent to 5.29 per cent) in fact do reflect the fundamentals. It’s not just the war in the Middle East and its impact on energy prices and America’s inflation rate that, at 3.4 per cent, remains well above the US Federal Reserve Board’s 2 per cent target.

Advertisement

As the year has progressed, bond investors have become increasingly focused on the actual underlying fundamentals: US government deficits and debt that have blown out at an accelerating rate. The deficit is about 6 per cent of GDP, and gross government debt just passed $US40 trillion within a $US32.5 trillion economy. The ‘knife to a gunfight’ analogy doesn’t come anywhere close to capturing the futility of Bessent’s efforts to manipulate the market. The market knows that America is on an unsustainable fiscal trajectory, and has begun pricing in that risk. The problem for Bessent is that the interest costs on that debt, already more than $US1 trillion and the third-largest expenditure item in the government’s budget behind social security and Medicare, are rising rapidly.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

US politics Alarms flashing red as Trump takes US debt to level almost beyond comprehension Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent Every time those longer-dated 10- and 30-year bonds, which were issued within a lower-rate environment, mature and have to be refinanced, they attract a higher interest rate and drive the overall interest cost to the government higher. That increased cost of “old” debt is occurring even as the Trump administration has added new debt, increasing the total amount of debt on issue by about $US4 trillion since Trump regained office last year. Bessent’s attempt to cap yields via the buybacks might, at best, influence a day or two’s trading, but is destined to fail. His buybacks, even if he were to significantly increase their size, are inconsequential when set against the scale of a $US32 trillion market that trades $US1 trillion a day. The “knife to a gunfight” analogy doesn’t come anywhere close to capturing the futility of Bessent’s efforts to manipulate the market.

Advertisement

His intervention to try to prop up the Japanese yen might be more successful, but only because the fundamentals in Japan are shifting, with its bond yields, previously suppressed by decades of the Bank of Japan’s raft of unconventional monetary policies, rising. The modest US involvement in a large-scale BoJ yen-buying splurge was also motivated by Bessent’s efforts to protect the US market, with fears that Japan might have to offload its vast US bondholding to fund its defence of its currency, adding to the pressure for higher US yields. Similarly, Bessent’s support for the Genius Act – which would provide the first legislative and regulatory framework for the issuance of stablecoins, and create a large new source of buying for US bonds – can be viewed in the context of his efforts to suppress the upwards trend in US yields, as could his relaxation of some big bank capital regulations. What’s developing in the bond market could be, and has been, regarded as a normalisation of US yields after nearly two decades of abnormal monetary policies. Yields have been far higher in the past – they were above 5 per cent leading into the global financial crisis – without it threatening US economic growth or corporate stability.

Advertisement

However, the difference between then and now is what happened in the aftermath of the financial crisis to the economic settings of not just the US, but most of the developed countries. To stave off deflation, and even a depression, governments embraced aggressive fiscal stimulus and their central banks, borrowing from Japan, embarked on unconventional monetary policies. Quantitative easing – central bank buying of bonds and mortgages to suppress interest rates – and other measures to control yield curves were widespread. The bond market could respond and take matters into its own hands if Trump’s appointed chair Kevin Warsh doesn’t follow his recent hawkish words with action. AP The yields on government debt were driven down to near or even below zero – investors were, in fact, paying some central banks to keep their funds safe – which made the build-up in government debt near costless. The Fed, and its peers, left those novel monetary policies in place for the best part of a decade. The Fed didn’t start its “quantitative tightening” – the running down of the piles of bonds and mortgages it had acquired – until 2017.

Advertisement

Until the pandemic, there were negligible inflation rates in the developed economies (economists were debating how to increase inflation), so interest rates remained low, encouraging debt-issuance and debt-driven investment strategies. Sharemarkets boomed and non-banks – hedge funds and private equity – and ordinary investors made effectively riskless gains on their leveraged trades. The pandemic saw central banks again slash interest rates and governments open the debt spigots wide. Once the worst of the pandemic was over, and the disruptions to global supply chains ignited inflation rates, the central bankers began reversing course, but governments kept expanding their balance sheets in what was still a low-rate environment. That’s why the “normalisation” of bond yields towards historic levels is a threat to US and other economies’ stability. Today’s normal doesn’t look like the pre-financial crisis past.

Advertisement

In 2007, the US had about $US9 trillion of debt in a $US15 trillion economy. Today, it has $US40 trillion debt in a $US32.5 trillion economy. On the International Monetary Fund’s numbers, global government debt in 2007 was about 44 per cent of global GDP; today it’s 94 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Bonds The world is in a debt spiral and alarm signals are going off Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Next week, the Fed’s Open Market Committee meets, with the benefit of inflation data that will be available later this week, to decide whether to raise the Fed’s policy rate. An increase might only validate what’s already occurred within the market, but it might also shift the yield curve up a notch. While continued Fed inaction might be rationalised, the bond market could respond and take matters into its own hands if Trump’s appointed chair Kevin Warsh doesn’t follow his recent hawkish words with action. An increase in the federal funds rate (the equivalent of the Reserve Bank’s cash rate) would infuriate Trump and, more particularly, have Warsh and Bessent’s policies not just diverging, but colliding.

Advertisement

If there is a conflict between Warsh’s policies and Bessent’s, the Fed, with the support of the bond market, would inevitably prevail. Even without the Fed’s encouragement, the bond market “vigilantes”, having emerged from almost two decades of relative dormancy in response to the explosive growth of US debt and deficits, will determine the future of US rates. Bessent might boast that “I am the house now” while warning traders not to bet against the yen because, he says, he has “asymmetric” information about what the BoJ and Japanese government plan to do. With Japan gradually moving in a direction that investors advocate and support, he might not be challenged on that assertion. In America, however, his inside information means little because the rising tides of deficits and debt and a rediscovered awareness, by bond investors at least, of the need to price for risk will overwhelm any attempts by the US Treasury to game the market. title: ‘Who blinks first’: Government and rowing at odds over 2032 venue
text:
Advertisement

NationalQueenslandBrisbane 2032 Olympics ‘Who blinks first’: Government and rowing at odds over 2032 venue Cameron Atfield September 10, 2026 — 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Queensland premier and his deputy have made a public show of force in Rockhampton to insist the Fitzroy River will host rowing events in 2032, after the sport’s world governing body cast doubt on its suitability to host Olympic competition. International rowing federations expressed scepticism of the plan during the World Rowing congress last week, which led to president Jean-Christophe Rolland to concede the governing body held concerns about the proposed venue. Standing near the banks of the Fitzroy River, Premier David Crisafulli said course testing was ongoing and he was confident it would get the “right result” for Olympic competition in 2032. All smiles: Premier David Crisafulli posted this image on social media in a public show of support for the Rockhampton Olympic rowing venue. David Crisafulli “Every so-called impediment that’s been put up has been dismissed by the people who live it and breathe and can understand it best,” he said.

Advertisement

“This is the last hurrah of people trying to find ways to, quite frankly, discredit something that makes a hell of a lot of sense, and we’re not for turning on this.” Crisafulli said Olympic rowing would be held in Rockhampton, “no ifs, no buts” – but there was a “but”. As QRowunion chairman Gary Merritt pointed out, the determination of whether the Fitzroy River was suitable for Olympic competition remained in the hands of World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee. “It is a case of who’s going to blink first,” Merritt said.

Advertisement

Referring to the City of Moreton Bay’s proposal for a purpose-built venue at an old quarry in Lawnton, Merritt said there was a “cheaper, better option” that would give more rowers a real legacy from the Olympic Games. “We’re going to spend all this money on a course in Rocky and, when the Olympics are over, there’s 150 people there who will use it – it’s not like we can take all of our big regattas up to Rocky. It’s just not going to happen,” he said. “It’s just going to be a huge white elephant and, in years to come, people are going to go, ‘What a waste of money that was.’” World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland has expressed concern about the course. Sebastian Kahnert/Getty Images But Merritt conceded rowing had missed the boat in not being able to present a fully formed proposal for the Moreton Bay facility in time for the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority’s 100-day review.

Advertisement

“We have to take some responsibility,” he said. “But having owned up to the fact that we didn’t have everything prepared as we should have, we’re now at a stage where we’re saying we can rescue the situation, but there’s just been no openness or any attempt to scrutinise what’s possible.” The proposed flatwater centre at Lawnton, with the Moreton Bay Indoor Sports Centre in the background. City of Moreton Bay If GIICA considered the Moreton Bay site, it did not rate a mention in its review. Rockhampton was considered, but GIICA rejected it as an option due to its “insufficient space for field of play and warm-up, inadequate onshore space and access road upgrade requirements, as well as limited accommodation options for athletes and officials”.

Advertisement

On the accommodation question, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said Olympic rowing would be the catalyst for more supply in the central Queensland city. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics Rocky rowing critics think they’re ‘too good for regional Queensland’: premier “With the accommodation, that’s a temporary overlay for the athletes’ village to house 1200 athletes – we’re in the process of working that out with [the Brisbane 2032 Organising Committee] and also GIICA,” he said. “We’re looking also at land activation programs, which is state-owned land, and how we can get houses on it, [and] hotel opportunities. “There’s a need for hotels right across regional Queensland – so many people are wanting to move and visit regional Queensland, so we need all that.”

Advertisement

Arguments against Rockhampton have ranged from its distance from the main Olympic hub in Brisbane, to an unfair field of play, and even the potential for crocodiles. Related Article Brisbane 2032 Olympics ‘Out of his depth’: Rowers escalate Rocky revolt against Bleijie In Rowing Queensland’s safety management plan for this month’s Queensland Schools’ Championship Regatta on the river, there are contingencies for crocodile sightings. “Upon receiving a ‘Crocodile Crocodile Crocodile’ call the following steps are to be carried out as quickly as possible,” the plans says. “Establish the nature of the emergency; Inform regatta control of sighting and location; Racing to be suspended; Competitors instructed to return to the bank; Officials ensure all boats are removed from the water.”

Gary Portelli believes his Theo Marks Stakes pair can push their claims for a run at the group 1 Epsom Handicap after overcoming feet problems. The Warwick Farm trainer has five-year-old mare Verona Rose and six-year-old gelding Encap first-up in the 1300m group 2 race at Rosehill on Saturday. Encap wins the Ming Dynasty in 2023. Getty Verona Rose finished last at her most recent outing, in the group 2 Emancipation Stakes on March 28. It was a disappointing end to a strong campaign taking in victory in the group 2 Guy Walter Stakes, third in the Triscay Stakes and fifth, less than a length and a half away, in the group 1 Coolmore Classic. “She pulled up very lame in the foot,” Portelli said of the Emancipation run.

Advertisement

“She had a foot abscess so she went back to the paddock. “She’d had a great preparation, it was just sad that we got to the grand final and we drew a horrible barrier, she got trapped wide and she never stretched out. She was gone before the home turn.” Portelli hopes to get Verona Rose back to her best and chase better black-type results. The $8 (TAB) chance has Zac Lloyd aboard and gate nine on Saturday. “She’s trialled really well, she seems in good order and she’s very good fresh,” Portelli said. “How she goes this weekend will determine whether we go uphill or across and stay at a level that sees her competitive every time she goes around.

Advertisement

Verona Rose wins the Guy Walter Stakes at Randwick in February. Getty Images “Every owner and trainer wants to get a group 1 placing, so if she comes back and races really well on the weekend, that would be something we would aim at ... maybe get into the Epsom light, or there’s the good mares’ race in Melbourne.” Encap has had two wins in his 31-start career, and both have come on the same annual program, taking out the Ming Dynasty Quality in 2023 and Theo Marks in 2024. He has placed in the Doncaster and Ingham during the drought since, and Portelli hoped he could rediscover his best on Saturday. He was $11 with Rachel King to ride from six. “Some horses come good certain times of the year, and hopefully this prep looks like it’s going to be a good one,” he said. “He’s trialled nicely and is very fresh. I’ve had a lot of trouble with his feet over the years, but it looks like we might be going in the right direction with him.

Advertisement

“He’s a nice horse who can come good over the mile at Randwick, so he might be a chance to get into the Epsom, but we’ll see how he goes first-up.” Portelli also has “rejuvenated” four-year-old Queen Of Clubs kicking off at Rosehill, where she was $23 in the Midway Handicap. A winner at two, Queen Of Clubs placed in the Silver Shadow Stakes in the spring but struggled in the autumn. “She didn’t really come up last prep like we were hoping, but from what I’m seeing at home, she’s going well,” he said. “Hopefully, she has a nice run to get her started then hopefully we’ll be stepping her up into some nice races. We are hoping she might be good enough to sneak into a Golden Eagle.”

title: ‘Malignant tumour’: FitzSimons on Jones
text:
WARNING: Graphic content

Author and columnist Peter FitzSimons has been cross-examined about his long-running and public dislike for former radio kingpin Alan Jones.

Mr FitzSimons is giving evidence in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney about his interactions with a man, who can only be known as Complainant C, who alleges Mr Jones kissed him without his consent and touched him on the penis on the outside of his clothing.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching and has continuously denied the allegations made by six male complainants.

C previously told the court that he first disclosed his allegations to Mr Jones' then-2GB stablemate Ray Hadley and Mr FitzSimons, a columnist and former rugby union player, in October 2019.

The court was previously told that at the time Mr FitzSimons was researching a story about Mr Jones.

C told the court he confided the allegations to Mr Hadley and soon after had a phone conversation with Mr FitzSimons, in which he repeated his claims.

Peter FitzSimons (left) is appearing as a star witness. Picture: NewsWire / Nikki Short

Alan Jones is standing trial in a Sydney court. Picture: NewsWire / Nikki Short

'A malignant tumour'

The court was told Mr FitzSimons' first contact with Mr Jones was in 1982 when he convinced him to come over to the Manly rugby club for the 1983 season.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr FitzSimons told the court that he considered Mr Jones a "genius rugby coach" but had written many columns critical of him.

The court was told Mr FitzSimons, in his newspaper column, had described Mr Jones as having "agendas", and accused him of "bullying" and "telling untruths".

Defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC put to Mr FitzSimons that he was "publicly and unashamedly anti-Jones".

"Almost proud," Mr FitzSimons replied.

Mr FitzSimons wrote of Mr Jones in one column: "Alan Jones is a malignant tumour on the body politic of this city, this state and this country and the sooner he is excised the better."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr FitzSimons told the court he was "very proud" of that quote.

Alan Jones is standing trial in a Sydney court. Picture: NewsWire/ Gaye Gerard.

'Gripping'

Mr FitzSimons told the court that C also alleged to him that Mr Jones touched him on the penis at a Sydney restaurant.

He said C relayed to him that Mr Jones asked that he sit next to him at the event, which was attended by others.

"Mr Jones's hand went onto his penis and he was gripping his penis," Mr FitzSimons said of what C told him.

He told the court that four days later he was told by Mr Hadley that C was "deeply upset", "panicking" and "spiralling".

He said he told Mr Hadley he would not pursue C's claim and would "leave him alone".

Mr FitzSimons told the court that he handed over his notes of the conversation to Sydney Morning Herald journalist Kate McClymont because he did not believe he could pursue the story.

Ray Hadley appeared as a witness during the trial. Picture: NewsWire / Nikki Short

'Romantically'

Mr FitzSimons told the court that during the October 16, 2019 phone call, C told him that Mr Jones kissed him in a lift at the broadcaster's Circular Quay apartment building, which is commonly known as The Toaster.

He said C told him that after a shopping trip, C's hands were fully laden with shopping bags.

Mr FitzSimons told the court that C said Mr Jones "pushed against him" and "grabbed him on the groin" and kissed him.

"He used the word 'romantically'," Mr FitzSimons told the court.

Mr Jones has denied the allegations made by the six male complainants. Picture: NewsWire / Nikki Short

'Revolted'

Mr FitzSimons appeared in court accompanied by a solicitor.

He told the court that during the call, C told him that while driving Mr Jones, the talkback host would put his hand on his knee, groin and penis.

"He made absolutely clear that he was revolted by what had happened," Mr FitzSimons said.

He told the court that the man was "deeply upset" that he had not told Mr Jones "no".

"He was very tearful … He was very, very upset. It was clear I was speaking to somebody who was completely emotionally traumatised," Mr FitzSimons said.

Alan Jones. Picture: NewsWire/ Nicholas Eagar

Peter FitzSimons. Picture: Supplied

During his conversation with Mr FitzSimons, C said he declined to give his name or tell his story publicly.

"I told (Mr FitzSimons) how Alan used to kiss me, how he used to touch me on the penis, how it happened when I was driving him," C told the court during his evidence last month.

"Peter asked me if I wanted to tell that story publicly and I immediately declined.

"At no point did I tell him who I was, at no point did I identify myself."

C ultimately aired his story publicly when he spoke to journalist Kate McClymont in late 2023.

The trial continues.

title: Worker crushed by bitumen roller
text:
A man is fighting for life after being crushed by a bitumen roller in Sydney's northwest.

The 62-year-old man was at a worksite on the M2 near the Beecroft Rd exit in Cheltenham about 10.45pm when he was crushed underneath a ride-on bitumen roller.

The sustained serious injuries to his abdomen, pelvis and right leg after being crushed by the four-tonne machinery.

A man is in critical condition after being crushed by a bitumen roller. Picture NewsWire/ Gaye Gerard

He was rushed to Royal North Shore Hospital in a critical condition.

The driver of the ride-on roller was taken to hospital for mandatory testing.

NewsWire has contacted SafeWork NSW for comment.
